subtopic: TENDER NO. 43-1-1977-D    STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR PARTICULARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Nipissing asked the Prime Minister whether he would look into tender No. 43-1-1977-D which closed on June 5, 1961, and give the particulars to the house.
This was a tender relating to plumbing pipe and pipe fittings, and was issued by the Ottawa district office of the Department of Defence Production. The low tender was submitted by Emco Limited at a price of $573.09. The products offered by Emco Limited were partially of Canadian manufacture and partially imported from the United Kingdom. The next lowest tender was submitted by Crane Limited which quoted $578.14 and offered products entirely manufactured in Canada.
The policy relating to procurement of defence supplies is as follows. With respect

to head office contracts, that is all contracts involving major production or procurement programs, every effort is made to ensure maximum Canadian content. For many of our most important contracts only Canadian manufacturers are invited to bid. In many other areas, preferences are given to Canadian contractors.
With respect to district office contracts, which normally relate to off the shelf items and where tenders are restricted to local manufacturers, jobbers, wholesalers, distributors and agents, the low bidder meeting the specifications is invariably selected. The district offices of the Department of Defence Production placed 130,000 contracts in the fiscal year 1960-61. It is obvious, therefore, that with respect to this very large number of contracts the only practical purchasing rule is to award the contract to the low bidder.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last evening I had been mentioning some problems on the estimates of the Department of Public Works. I should like to congratulate the government in this connection, but I think I should not really congratulate them because in my opinion they got into this situation by accident rather than by design. I refer to the field of housing in which the government now finds itself.
If it had not been for the money that was put into housing by the federal government several years ago there just would have been no home building at all in Canada. It was an indication that something was wrong with the source of the money upon which we were depending for the expansion of our housing industry in Canada when the government- and certainly this is true of the Conservative government-had to go into the field of lending of money for housing.
I do not think this has been a bad move; I think it has been a very good one. Indications are now apparent that other interests would like to put money into housing and that there will be an expansion of credit, and mortgage money particularly, available for housing. This has been a good thing. If this government have done anything to solve the unemployment problem across this country, probably their greatest effort has been in the field of housing. The fact that the federal government did put money into housing when money was not available from other

Supply-Public Works
sources and when no building was taking place in other fields has meant a great deal of employment in the housing industry itself and, second, in the service trades that depend upon the housing industry.
This brings us, of course, to another problem that has now developed. The minister has indicated that he is going to unload a large number of mortgages now being held by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It is my opinion that this in itself may not be a bad thing either. However, I think we are going to have to look very carefully at this matter, and for this reason we have been watching very closely one of the bills on the order paper being sponsored by a private member. This bill is in connection with secondary mortgages and the handling of mortgages by means other than those by which they have been handled in the past. We have been interested in this, and I have satisfied myself that this government is not invading the field that the minister has indicated he is going to leave open for industry and the financial interests to take part in.
I only want to make this suggestion. The federal government has not done a bad job in housing. It has not hurt the government; it has not hurt the Conservative party, and I think it has been good for the country. Therefore I think it behooves us to give consideration to going into this matter more deeply, rather than getting out of it entirely. For this reason I hope when the minister brings in the resolution that will indicate a bill is in the offing for the establishment of a secondary mortgage field, he will give consideration to a crown corporation handling secondary mortgages. I believe it is highly essential for the development of Canada that we take the profit motive out of the mortgage field and the interest that is available when going into such an important field as national housing. The lower the rate of interest on that money, the more money is available and the easier it is to obtain. In this way we would have the largest amount of money available for housing, whether it be through secondary mortgages or the original Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans. Both tend to increase housing development in Canada, and this is a vital necessity even now.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to congratulate the minister for the work his department has done recently in the construction of some of the very lovely small federal buildings. I was very pleased to have the opportunity of attending the opening of a post office, in the company of the hon. member for Cape Breton South, in my riding two weeks ago, and

should like to state that it is a very lovely building. It is very modern and designed to serve the needs of that community for some time in the future. I feel there was a good deal of foresight in the planning of this building, in that it has been designed in such a way as to allow for a good deal of expansion without, at the same time, creating a future white elephant. If expansion does not take place as quickly as has been anticipated I feel that building can still be used in an efficient way.
The construction of this building also created extra employment in that area during the wintertime, which has been a tremendous advantage to the people of that community. I am very pleased that this government, through the Department of Public Works, has seen fit to provide this type of opportunity to various communities, because this has been of tremendous help in providing employment for a number of people in this country.
I suggest there are many other fields of endeavour in which this department should take part. There are many problems in my own area of which I am aware and which I should like to bring to the attention of the department when considering the relevant votes. However, at this time I should like to comment in a general way in respect to the government's building activities in the Ottawa area.
While it is fine for an hon. member to say in this house that there are $17 million worth of government buildings in his riding-and I refer to the constituency of Russell-I do not feel it is necessarily a good thing. The centennial of Canada's confederation is not far away. I feel that this country has now reached that stage where Canadians can be proud of it, and that now is the time for us to review and correct the haphazard building program that has been followed in the city of Ottawa.
At the outset I should like to say that I do not believe the central experimental farm should be developed as a land assembly scheme upon which government buildings should be built in haphazard fashion. I realize that certain ministers of the crown would like to see many types of government buildings built on that farm, but I believe the experimental farm has served and is serving a useful purpose, and should not be cluttered up with departmental buildings of all types. I suggest the government should use some foresight in its planning and location of government buildings, so that over the period of the next 50 or 100 years this city will be developed in a manner and style in which we as Canadians can take pride.
The city of Ottawa itself is the national capital of Canada and should not be developed

as an industrial city but as a national capital. I realize that the federal government must compensate this city for the industrial losses which will accompany the development of the city as a national capital, but I suggest the federal government must have some authority as well as interest in this type of development program of development which is being followed at this time has resulted in the location Wellington street in order that at least the administrative headquarters of each department of government may be located there. The program of development which is being followed at this time has resulted in the location of many administrative buildings in the outlying areas of the city.
I feel this is a mistake on the part of the government. For instance, an individual coming to Ottawa with the intention of perhaps discussing a contract with the officials of the Department of Public Works will have difficulty in locating the officials of that department. I suggest he will probably have to take a taxi on a tour through Tunney's pasture and various other government building locations before finally arriving at the new public works building in the area of Hog's Back. I know I have difficulty locating these officials even by telephone from my own office, and therefore suspect that a subcontractor from an area such as Timiskaming, perhaps the city of Kirkland Lake, being a stranger in Ottawa would have great difficulty in locating the officials of the department in which he is interested.
In making this suggestion I realize, of course, that many of the operations of different departments cannot properly be located close to parliament hill. I do not suggest that the technical services provided by the department of research, for example, should be located in downtown Ottawa, but at least the administration offices of that department could be located there.
If the government did expropriate all the property along Wellington street it could accomplish two things. It could rid that district of the slum areas which exist there, and could centralize the administration buildings of all departments of government. An individual visiting this city could then easily locate the officials of this government without the necessity of taking a taxi on a grand tour of the city. I believe an individual wishing to consult a deputy minister should not be expected to travel to the outskirts of the city in order to do so. After all, Canada is no longer a small country, and should have a national capital designed after the examples set by other nations of the world. I suggest the location of government buildings in Washington provides a good example for us to follow. That city has been designed and developed as
Supply-Public Works
the national capital of the United States. Here in Ottawa there exist all kinds of slums, industries, government departmental buildings, in all areas.
I suggest that the officials responsible for the development of Ottawa as a national capital should consult with the officials of the city of Ottawa in order to work out an efficient and effective plan for the development of the national capital. I seriously suggest to the minister for his consideration a program of expropriating the property along Wellington street so the administrative offices of this government could be centrally located. I also repeat my suggestion that the experimental farm be maintained as an experimental farm. I suggest the operation of that farm has been of great benefit to many people of this country over the years, through the development of better seeds and so on, and has provided solutions to various other agricultural problems which have existed. I suggest that a great deal of beneficial research and development has been carried out as a result of the operation of this farm. I strongly suggest this should not be a land assembly plan. I dislike very much going out to the experimental farm and finding that the federal government has erected a new building there because it had not bothered to expropriate additional land.
I should like to raise another problem with the minister. The minister may say it does not come under his jurisdiction. It is somewhat like the argument we had last night on the roads to resources program. I am speaking of the port of Moosonee. On page 11 of the report of the Department of Public Works we find the following statement:
As in previous years, members of the branch made several on-site surveys of various harbours. The interdepartmental group, consisting of senior officials of the Departments of Public Works, and Transport, continued to investigate major harbour requirements.
The people of northern Ontario are greatly interested in the survey now being carried out jointly by the federal and provincial governments having to do with the development of a northern salt water seaport, the only salt water seaport the province of Ontario can have. I refer to the port of Moosonee. The potential of that area is exceedingly great. Some of the largest iron ore deposits in the world are there. The potential of other minerals in the Moosonee area is great. We are very interested in seeing a comprehensive and legitimate survey conducted there.
In northern Ontario we have a railway owned by the provincial government. It was originally called the northern Ontario development railroad, and was built to open up the resources of northern Ontario. For many years

Supply-Public Works
Colonel Reynolds, the chairman of this railroad-he is now getting to be a very old man -pushed the idea of a salt water port at Moosonee for the development of northern Ontario.
This is not a pipe dream; it is a feasible thing. I believe that on many occasions the chairman of the railway used it for political purposes. I am quite sure that most of the politicians in northern Ontario have used it for political purposes. I have. I make one exception; the hon. member for Cochrane has never used it for political purposes, and it is in his riding. But I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Cochrane is very interested in the port of Moosonee. He has been going there for many years, and is well aware of the potential of the area.
A survey has been made. Press reports indicate that the minister has given assurance that the report will be made very shortly. Last night I looked up references in Hansard. The last one, which was a month old, indicated that the minister would be willing to bring in a report on the survey within a month. I presume the report of the survey is now available and that the minister's department has participated in it.
I think these things should be done by the federal government. I am not too pleased about anything the provincial government does in this field. In the field of harbours, lakes, navigable waters, and so on, the provincial government has shown a very narrow minded and provincial attitude toward those developments. It has decided that any waters throughout the province should be used for provincial parks and that those provincial parks should cost a great deal of money if you wish to visit them. Three years ago it cost you $1 to go to a provincial park in Ontario. Now it costs you $3 to go to a provincial park for the season. It costs $1 to stay in a provincial park.
Most of our navigable waters in northern areas that originally came under the jurisdiction of the federal government are now administered by the department of lands and forests of the provincial government. I strongly suggest that the minister keep his hand in this particular field, because it is my opinion that we get better utilization of some of our natural resource development if it is handled by the federal government than we do from the provincial government, particularly in those fields in which both governments are interested.
I should like the minister to give a full report on what is going to happen at Moosonee. We know it is an extensive development proposition. It is a proposition that would have a high labour content and would do a great deal for the development of that area.

It also has a national defence aspect because if an enemy force was going to land it would find it most advantageous to come in through Hudson strait, Hudson bay and down through James bay, and it would then be fewer than 600 miles from the main industrial city of Canada, namely Toronto. If for no other reason, we should develop this port for defence purposes.
However, in my opinion defence is only an excuse. It is something I would use with the minister as an argument because the government seems to give consideration to this type of argument. If we developed our resources in that area we would increase our secondary development, because we would be serving the communities and the industries which would develop from the use of the natural resources. This would carry far more weight with the people of northern Ontario and I think the people of Canada in general than anything else.
This proposed development has been a political football. It has been kicked around for a long time. I have been there; I have looked at the terrain. I am no engineer. I do not know whether it is feasible or not, but I do know this. If the port is feasible it would do a great deal for the people of northern Ontario. It would mean new life for Kirkland Lake and for all the towns along the Ontario Northland Railway. It would add new life to the agricultural development which is taking place in the little clay belt. It would mean a tremendous development program in probably the largest undeveloped agricultural area in Canada today, the great clay belt which covers nearly all of Cochrane north. In my opinion all these things would take place if a port is feasible and could be developed at Moosonee.
The survey which is being done under the direction of the minister's department is of such importance that it will give guidance toward the development of the resources of northern Ontario for many years to come. If it is at all possible to develop a seaport in northern Ontario, then it should be developed and the minister should give not only his assistance and his guidance but his whole-hearted support. I see the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources in his seat, I do not know whether an opportunity has been afforded to him so early in his term of office to visit the area of northern Ontario of which I am speaking, but if he does visit it I am sure he will be impressed with the resources that are available in that area. This was part of his predecessor's vision. It is a part of the vision that is possible of realization. It is part of the vision that is feasible. It is quite within

the realm of development in the next few years as the kind of community that his predecessor spoke of, namely development much farther north.
What will be done hinges on the reply of the minister. I hope he will find his way clear to give consideration to this development at this time. The people of northern Ontario are frightened at the situation which is developing. They see their basic industry, gold and silver mining, reaching the stage where most mining companies are nearing the end of the properties they are now working. They have not been able to obtain any assurance from the government that there will be an increase in the price of their product, so this development is a vital nec-cessity. If they are to plan for a constructive future they are going to have to take into consideration the availability of a market not only south from their communities but north as well.

Mr. Chairman, there is much I should like to say about the minister's estimates in this committee, but given to brevity as I am I shall have to put in capsule form some of my thoughts about what the minister has done in the area which I have the honour to represent. We are very pleased with the continuing major programs in the Wood islands area, which has become a very important point in our transportation link with the province of Nova Scotia. If, as we hope, a new boat is placed in that run there is no reason why there should not be night service, and the Department of Public Works would be called upon to do even more in the way of providing facilities.
The hon. member for Timiskaming spoke about housing. We in Prince Edward Island are just beginning to take advantage of some of the federal opportunities in the housing field, and we look forward to most helpful developments along this line.
A project very close to our hearts at the present time is the construction of a new railway wharf, as we call it, at Charlottetown. The present one is being overtaxed by the increase in shipping which has come about in recent years in Prince Edward Island. At the present time our trade, especially with the northern ports along the St. Lawrence, is expanding greatly.
In Prince Edward Island we are looking forward to a great celebration in 1964. Many people, we hope, will be coming to Charlottetown by boat, and I hope the minister's new wharf will be completed at that time.
I listened with interest the other night as the hon. member for Halifax spoke about an event that took place there nearly 100 years ago. I might say, of course, that the event
Supply-Public Works
he spoke of was a mere postscript to the Charlottetown conference of 1864 which planned the confederation of this great country. The Minister of Public Works is involved now, however, in that question which down through the years has been the most important political and economic question to the people of Prince Edward Island. I refer to a transportation link between our province and the mainland, between Borden and Cape Tormentine.
It was this very question of transportation which assumed major importance in the confederation negotiations of 1873, and the province of Prince Edward Island exacted from the dominion government a guarantee of continuous and efficient communication. There has been much discussion about this in the years that have passed. In 1903, for instance, for 40 days and 40 nights nobody travelled to Prince Edward Island. No mail came or left, and when the Prince Edward Island members eventually got to Ottawa they had something to say about this situation. In 1907, from three o'clock in the afternoon of one day until one o'clock the following morning, the subject of Prince Edward Island transportation was before this chamber.
The Minister of Public Works need have no fear that we shall discuss it that long on this occasion, but he has become involved in this historically significant, politically potent and economically vital factor because of the survey for the causeway. I suppose he would hardly expect me to be on my feet for any length of time without mentioning the causeway. I should like to take this opportunity now to say what I have said to him privately, how much the people of Prince Edward Island appreciate the visit by his very able and competent deputy minister, General Young, who came to Charlottetown about a year ago, spoke to a group of citizens there and gave a most excellent and lucid report on the causeway survey up to that time.
We are very anxious that this matter be pressed forward with all the speed possible having in mind the tremendous technological and scientific considerations which must be involved in a project of such magnitude and such originality. We realize that it is a tremendous undertaking. At one time we were hearing stories about remedial measures that must be taken with respect to various parts of the shore line on the south shore of Prince Edward Island. Indeed, at one time I heard that one area which would be destined for inundation was the area around the very beautiful community of Victoria which happens to be my home town and birthplace. In this instance I had no desire to become a postdiluvian survivor. However, we learn from

Supply-Public Works
the reports so far made that this matter has been dealt with and the problem has been taken in stride.
I was tremendously impressed a while ago when I went to the national research council and saw the model study. I knew this was an engineering project of great magnitude but to see it visibly before me, to have it explained by some of the finest engineers not only in Canada but in other parts of the world as well, was a most valuable educative opportunity. We in Prince Edward Island may sometimes be regarded as impatient about the causeway survey. We are quite aware that great sums have been expended and much research has been done. If, however, the Minister of Transport will provide us with another new car ferry to replace the Prince Edward Island, this will contribute to an abatement of our impatience but not to the lessening of our interest or our desire for this up-to-date communication link.
When the time comes I think it will be easy to prove the economic feasibility of the causeway. As one looks at the tremendously rising cost of ferries he will see that the demand for service will require more and more boats, and the more boats that are put in service the higher the cost will rise. With the development of a land link between our province and the mainland, one could predict that with the increasing traffic the unit costs would go down.
That there is an extensive increase in traffic I need hardly point out. As late as 1943 we had coming to Prince Edward Island in one year 9,539 automobiles. In 1960 this had risen to 171,540. There is every indication that the season ahead of us will be our finest tourist season yet. As more and more people learn the glories of our province we can predict that on an ever ascending scale we shall have people wanting to get to Prince Edward Island and sad to have to leave it. Therefore we will require the most up-to-date transportation link possible.
I believe that the most up-to-date link will be a causeway. We realize the magnitude of the project. While at times we may be impatient, our impatience will be abated, as I say, if we have a new boat. I know that the minister and the officials who are working with him will want to make no mistake. We got quite a shaking in Prince Edward Island last winter. It was the worst winter we have undergone since 1903 or 1905. There is some uncertainty as to which was the worst. There is still some ice not too far removed from the gulf area. The heavy formation of ice which remained there month after month would certainly have to be one of the factors, and an obvious factor, in the

consideration of building this tremendous and imaginative link of our province with the mainland.
I am convinced of the seriousness of the study being undertaken. I am convinced of its magnitude, although as a layman I would not pretend that I understand all the ramifications. I know the minister will persevere in this effort, and that every possible avenue will be explored in examining the economic and engineering feasibility of this project. I do not suppose we could have it ready for 1964 for our celebration, so we might be content to wait for the other confederation celebration in 1967.
There is much more I might say about the initiative the minister has demonstrated in his department which has meant so much to the people in my province, but I am content to rest my case on the causeway at this moment. I know the minister has heard a great deal about the causeway from hon. members from Prince Edward Island, and no doubt the hon. lady from that province who recently joined us will present her views to the minister shortly.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to bring up a matter that is of great interest to the hon. member for Niagara Falls and to myself, having to do with the deepening of that part of the Welland river between Port Robinson and Chippawa on the Niagara river. In years gone by this part of the Welland river formed part of the Welland canal and therefore was navigable. Today it is filled up, and I doubt that even small barges could navigate this part of the river.
I have received many representations recommending this. Recently I received representations in this respect from the township of Crowland, copies of which I have sent to the minister. In years past when Niagara Falls was part of my riding I received representations from the chamber of commerce of that city and from different plants in the area. I might say that the Welland river crosses under the Welland ship canal at Welland through an aqueduct. For some miles the Welland river and the Welland canal run closely parallel.
Some years ago representatives of the Niagara Falls chamber of commerce came to Ottawa and proposed the construction of a dock at Port Robinson which would serve both the Welland river and the Welland canal. In other words, these two streams are sufficiently close that the same dock could serve both of them. If one were constructed goods could be unloaded from boats in the Welland canal to ships on the Welland river and vice versa.
As I have indicated, this part of the Welland river was at one time part of the Welland

canal. When the canal was first built it ran from Port Dalhousie to Port Robinson. There was a lockage into the Welland river. In later years, of course, a cut was dredged from Port Robinson to Port Colborne and the Welland river was deserted as far as navigation was concerned. There are a number of plants situated along this river at the present time. I have been told that these would make use of waterborne traffic. This area is an excellent location for the settlement of industry.
In making representations to the government concerning the dock the chamber of commerce presented an outline of an ideal situation, namely to have a lockage between the Welland canal and the Welland river at Port Robinson. At the time the representations were made we were told that the government did not have any money. I suppose it is accurate to say that the government has less money today that it had then. It is therefore perhaps futile to press for this lockage project at this time. I would, however, urge the minister to look into the situation with a view to bringing about conditions under which we might have navigation in this part of the Welland river.

Mr. Chairman, in the few
minutes at my disposal, I should like to deal with the trans-Canada highway which runs through my constituency.
Last January, I stated publicly that the building of the trans-Canada highway by way of He aux Tourtes would cost from $9 to $15 million more than the route proposed previously through lie Perrot and Dorion.
At that time, neither plans nor specifications had yet been drawn up to enable the provincial minister of highways, the Hon. Bernard Pinard, to submit specific estimates for the new route going through lie aux Tourtes. Therefore, in order to have this change in route approved by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), in Ottawa, Mr. Pinard sent him a telegram which reads as follows:
(Text):
Following the Information given to your Mr. Williams, assistant deputy minister, and to your Mr. G. T. Clarke, concerning the route of the trans-Canada highway at the western end of Montreal island could you wire me immediately your authorization to announce officially the new route which is to go through lie aux Tourtes instead of lie Perrot. This will help me very much in the preparation of my estimates for the next fiscal year. The change recommended in the route may save your government several hundred thousands of dollars.
(Translation):
So the reason put forward by Hon. Mr. Pinard to have the route changed, was to enable the federal government to make substantial savings.
Supply-Public Works
A minister of the Quebec provincial government who defends the interests of the federal government! That is unique.
Last January 17, before the change in the route was made public, I telephoned the Hon. Rene Levesque, the Minister of Public Works for the province of Quebec who is responsible for the construction of bridges.
I told him that if he wanted to build a bridge between the island of Montreal and the Vaudreuil-Soulanges riding by going through lie aux Tourtes, he would have to secure beforehand the authorization from the federal departments of public works and transport.
I added that such an authorization could be obtained-

When I phoned the Hon. Rene Levesque at Quebec on January 17 last, I told him that, if it was his intention to have a bridge built over the Ottawa river between the island of Montreal and He aux Tourtes, he would have to get permission or authorization from the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport, in Ottawa, for the simple reason that the Ottawa river is a navigable river.
At that moment, the provincial government thought that, if the bridge was built there, a causeway could be erected at the eastern end and another one from lie aux Tourtes, which would have considerably reduced the length of the bridge.
I pointed out then to Mr. Levesque that such a project would bring dangers of flood from the Prairies river as well as from the Mille lies river. Moreover it would have an influence on the water level in Montreal harbour, while diverting the water from the Ottawa river.
Well, Mr. Chairman, that is what I told the Hon. Rene Levesque on January 17 last for the sole purpose of giving him a good piece of advice so that he would not look foolish in making the statements he intended to make.
He replied that I did not know what I was talking about, that I was no engineer and that it was his business.
A few days later, it was announced that the route would go through lies aux Tourtes

Supply-Public Works
instread of lies Perrot. On the first of February last, I made a public statement which appeared a few days afterward in La Presse.
In that letter, I gave some particulars on the additional work which the new route would involve and it is only following that article that borings were undertaken by the minister of public works of the province of Quebec, on the Ottawa river.
It is since then also that work on the trans-Canada highway has been stopped, that is to say plans have not been drawn up, specifications are not ready, and I think that the minister will admit that work on the trans-Canada highway in the Vaudreuil-Soulanges district will not start this year, precisely because the route was changed, that the lie aux Vaches route, which had been recognized on November 28 last when the federal and1 the provincial governments signed an agreement with regard to the trans-Canada highway was abandoned. Moreover when that route was changed, the data or recommendations of certain engineers in the province of Quebec were found not to be in accordance with the facts.
With regard to the lie aux Tourtes route, it was discovered that the bottom on which piles could be erected is at 40, 60 and even 80 feet below the water-level, whereas for the lie aux Vaches route, the solid ground which could carry the piles, is found at about eight to 10 feet below the water-level.
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to hold up the house any longer with this matter, but as the federal government has agreed with the province to settle the issue of the trans-Canada highway, and as an amount of $22 million is now available to the province of Quebec for the building of that highway, and as the worst traffic problem in the province of Quebec, outside Montreal, is precisely found between lie Perrot and Dorion, I think it is imperative that the federal government and the government of the province of Quebec get the work started on the trans-Canada highway in the area I represent.
Recently, the provincial government offered to take over the Soulanges canal. It promised certain developments for sportsmen and fishermen in the area. But so long as the problem of the trans-Canada highway has not been solved in the constituency of Vaudreuil-Soulanges, I think it would be unwise and indeed would show a lack of foresight to carry out developments for the benefit of sportsmen while the major traffic problem remains unsolved, because development will be impossible in my constituency until it is solved.

I therefore urge the Minister of Transport or the Minister of Public Works to do their utmost to persuade the provincial government or the provincial minister of highways to get the work started as soon as possible on the trans-Canada highway and on the bridges, whether it be at lie aux Tourtes or lie aux Vaches.

I am rising in order, first, to add some remarks to those of the hon. member for Welland with respect to a proposal which for some years has been placed before the department, as to the deepening of the Welland river and ultimately locking it into the Welland canal system in order to provide a navigable waterway into the heartland of the area which I have the honour to represent.
Along the Welland river, which at present is a broad and pleasant stream but of no assistance to industry in the area, there are several major industries. One has been located within the past year within the riding of Welland; I refer to the Ford of Canada glass plant. In addition, there is a very large plant which was built by this government during the war years and was later acquired by North American Cyanamid, Limited. There are two other major industries, and all these industries have a substantial transportation problem.
While the Niagara area is perhaps the shining diamond in the golden horseshoe, as southern Ontario has been referred to, not only because of its natural wonders but also because of its industrial development, it is hampered considerably in its industrial development by the lack of transportation facilities. It has not benefited from the development of the seaway, and under the present situation it cannot benefit from it. However, if there were to be constructed a locking device to lock in the Welland river and the Welland canal, this would open cheap water transportation to major industries located along the canal by permitting them to get into the St. Lawrence seaway system.
It is my understanding that over the years representations have been made to the minister and his predecessor by municipalities both in the riding of Niagara Falls and the riding of Welland, and also that representations have been made by chambers of commerce and interested individuals. So far as I am aware, no study has ever been made on the governmental level as to the cost of such a development. But since I know that

the minister responsible for this department is particularly interested in the development of southern Ontario, and since I know that he is a part of a government who have confessed that their greatest interest is in the expansion of this country, I suggest that a study might be made in the department with a view to assisting this area by the development of this proposal.
There are other matters in the riding of Niagara Falls which have already come to the attention of the minister. One of these was raised by my predecessor in the years 1957 and 1958; and during the hiatus of a few months last year when my riding was not represented, the hon. member for Lincoln was kind enough to continue the matter until I was elected. I refer to the representations which have been made to the Department of Public Works by the municipality of Crystal Beach. Crystal Beach is a village located on the lake. It is perhaps one of the greatest tourist attractions of a man made nature in my riding. It is a small village in the wintertime but develops greatly in the summertime. I am informed that the banks in the area have estimated that something in the order of a quarter of a million dollars in United States currency comes into the country as a result of operations there.
Within the past year or so the municipality has made great exertions to extend its facilities for tourists, particularly tourists from other countries. Over the past two years representations have been made to the Department of Public Works with a view to having a breakwater installed in order that a small boat harbour or marina might be constructed at Crystal Beach. In this particular area there are many very fine sand beaches and there is a great deal of small boating. However, nowhere in the area is there a location where they may harbour.
Representations have been made over the past few years, and most recently over the past winter, to the department. They have suggested that a consultant be called in to clear the matter of sewage disposal in the area. The municipality has constructed a new road right down to water level and has made strong representations, as I said, under the aegis of the then warden of the county of Welland, a noted friend of the government, and also through the hon. member for Lincoln in order to have this marina brought about. If the minister is interested in the development of what I think has become the third greatest industry in Canada, namely the tourist industry, I suggest that for a very small expenditure on behalf of the people of Canada a very large return can be obtained by assistance in the construction of this breakwater and small boats harbour.
Supply-Public Works
I can tell the minister that I will be making representations from time to time on this matter. I have photographs which I am sure are already in his files. There will be delegations here from time to time. We intend to press the minister for this installation. I would hope that he would see the benefit that would accrue to the area and to the country generally from a small expenditure.
I venture to make these representations to the minister because he is known as the most sweet tempered, most considerate and most thoughtful man in the House of Commons. I think this is demonstrated by the fact that in the public works estimates for the whole province of Ontario for this year, Niagara Falls rejoices in having the second largest commitment.
I shall have some remarks to make later when other items are called. However, I wish to congratulate the minister on having demonstrated so clearly that party bias or partisanship is not at all a factor in his make-up. Notwithstanding the fact that Niagara Falls riding has been well represented in the past by those of my political persuasion, the minister has seen fit to put in his estimates this year the sum of something in excess of one third of a million dollars expenditure in my area. For this the minister has my gratitude.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I should like to extend to the minister my sincere thanks for the tremendous assistance he has provided me and my constituents, especially in the Springhill area, by seeing that they are to be given a new federal building, thereby indicating to the people of that town that they certainly have not been forgotten by the people in Ottawa, especially those in the minister's department, and that we believe they will continue to progress and attain a stable economy, which they certainly deserve.
I should also like to thank the minister for the tremendous assistance he has provided the fishermen in my area through harbour improvements that are now under way at Spencer's Island, Parrsboro and Wallace, and which are to be under way shortly at Mala-gash, Joggins and Port Greville. There is no doubt that these improved harbour facilities will be of tremendous value to the fishermen in their work.
May I at this time bring to the minister's attention the need for a new fishermen's wharf at Pugwash. I know the minister has given favourable consideration to this matter, but has been delayed awaiting the decision of the salt mines there as to the loading of salt on vessels which will then take this product to other areas of Canada and

Supply-Public Works
the United States. I would, however, urge upon the minister the need for making a decision with regard to the fishermen's wharf. Certainly the fishermen of this booming community are in need of better facilities and I feel they should have them at the earliest possible date.
I should now like to turn to another matter of great importance to all people in the maritime provinces. I refer to the Chignecto canal and the report which the people are awaiting in this regard. I know there were delays in establishing the committee that was to consider the reports prepared for the Chignecto canal committee. In this regard I wish to commend the minister for his attitude on the selection of personnel for this committee. Certainly it would not have been right or proper to have people who had already committed themselves to this project then being placed on the committee to determine whether or not it was feasible.
I do not think the reports when completed could have been given that regard that will now be possible with the civil servants who are there to assess this matter in an impartial manner and determine whether or not the construction of the canal is feasible. I do, however, want to point out to the minister that we are very anxious to see this report completed and provided to the public in order that they might decide whether or not this is the type of project that should be proceeded with immediately. I personally am most anxious to see whether the report that was prepared for the Chignecto canal committee is sound and whether the proposals set forth therein can be confirmed by this committee.
If it should be that the findings of this interdepartmental committee of officials of the federal government and the government of New Brunswick do not confirm those set forth in the reports prepared for the canal committee, there must be a reappraisal of the whole matter. However, if the earlier reports are confirmed I feel that we must give very serious consideration to the immediate construction of the canal. In this regard I would certainly appreciate the minister's comments on where the committee's work now stands and just when we "will have a report available on this very important and urgent matter.

Mr. Chairman, I just have a few brief general remarks to make at this time, one of them having to do with the total amount of money estimated to be expended this year compared with the estimates of this department for other years. I refer to the 1957-58 estimates. These are the main estimates, and I am not taking

into account the various supplementary estimates that have been introduced during these particular years. In 1957-58 we discover that the main estimates of the department totalled $145 million. I am just speaking in round figures rather than giving the exact amount. You will recall, Mr, Chairman, that the estimates for 1958-59 had perhaps something to do with an election that was also in the offing. For that year we find this department boosted its estimated expenditures to $172 million. This is not taking into account statutory items, which also increase and change from time to time.
In the fiscal year 1959-60 the estimates remained substantially the same. There was a slight increase, to $173 million. Then in the last fiscal year, 1960-61, they undoubtedly felt the influence of Mr. Coyne in this department. As least, if we can take at face value what the Minister of Finance said the other day, it is undoubtedly Mr. Coyne's fault that we had a decrease in the estimates of this department to $147 million, practically back to the figure for 1957-58. You will also remember, Mr. Chairman, that this was undoubtedly connected with those large blue pencils which the Minister of Finance passed out to all the departments of government when he wanted to balance the budget, and in fact I think initially balanced it, at least on paper, to within $12 million.
Oh, he was going to be $12 million over.

Yes, he would have a few dollars in his pocket. Of course subsequent events proved just how inept and wrong was the Minister of Finance, when he came along for the last fiscal year with five separate sets of supplementary estimates and we found that the original $12 million that he had estimated would be cash in the pocket, as it were, really ended up as a great indebtedness. I am quite sure that the activities of Mr. Coyne caused this curtailment and foolishness on the part of the Minister of Finance, who is thinking in terms of a balanced budget primarily to paint a picture of economic development in this nation. We are now considering the estimates of public works for the present fiscal year.
The year of expansion.

Yes, for the year of expansion. We find that the amount to be expended by the Department of Public Works has increased by $20 million over the amount for the last fiscal year. Next Tuesday evening, when the Minister of Finance presents his long awaited budget, perhaps we will learn something more about the so-called expansion which is to take place. I am not sure how much faith we

can place in that budget, in view of the past mistakes and blunders which have been made. However, there is an indication in the increase in the estimates of this department, to be expended on various projects, totalling $166 million, that some expansion will take place, and one can draw all kinds of conclusions regarding the necessity of this type of program.
I have very often considered the operations of the departments of public works, federal and provincial, as election operations, because these departments often delay the commencement of projects in various areas until such time as they coincide with an election. In this way the government is able to create the impression in the minds of the voters in the country that it is stepping into the economic field and providing measures of assistance, and that all one has to do is vote for that party and the building, wharf or whatever the project happens to be will be commenced.
I have also considered these departments of public works as kind of pork barrel departments. I do not indicate that is the case in this instance, but in the past I have considered this department of public works as being one that can be dipped into from time to time for political purposes. Perhaps the activities which have taken place recently in the province of Quebec will be the last of this kind that we will see.
The Department of Public Works is engaged in a field of activity which economists have recently classified as social capital activities; that is, public money being expended in regard to such things as roads, bridges, federal buildings, docks, shipping facilities and the like. In this regard we had an announcement from this government some time ago to the effect that in order to assist the economic conditions of various depressed areas, it was necessary to engage in what is classified as double depreciation to attract the establishment of industries. In considering this field of social capital activity one finds that the amount of social capital is inadequate and its use in many respects is obsolescent, particularly in view of the rapidly expanding urban areas.
We are in a continuing danger of choking out economic growth with congestion, pollution, the development of slums, and with the effects of deficiencies in vital public services and amenities. The bottlenecks appear to lie in the methods of financing, in lack of planning, and in the difficulties of achieving effective co-operation between the three levels of government.
That statement appears in the fifth report of the special committee of the Senate on manpower and employment, which can be found in the Senate Hansard of June 14, at page 876. I use it to succinctly point out the feeling which exists in many part of this
Supply-Public Works
country that there is a great deal to be desired in respect to activities in this field of so-called social capital.
The Department of Public Works expends a great deal of money in this field of social capital activity. However, it was the Senate of this country which commenced a study in regard to unemployment because this government failed to give that question proper consideration, and, in fact, even rejected suggestions last session that there was a necessity for considering the unemployment situation. The committee of that other place felt that the role of government in this field of social capital investment was in many respects obsolescent because of the development of slums, congestion, pollution and the like.
I suggest that we review the expenditures to be made by this department with a view to determining what effect these expenditures are liable to have upon our economy. Surely the government must realize-it has in past years, as has been indicated by explanations given to this house in glowing terms regarding the expenditure of moneys for housing development to meet unemployment situations -what effect the expenditure of this money in all the activities carried on by this department has had on the growth and expansion of our economy. I think we should analyse this situation to see what effect the spending of these moneys has on our economy, and to find out whether that committee on manpower and employment is accurate in its analysis of the situation.
As I have said, the report of that committee suggests that the bottlenecks appear to lie in the methods of financing, in the lack of planning, and in the difficulties of achieving effective co-operation among the three levels of government. I do believe there has been a lack in planning in this regard. I think this was illustrated by the Minister of Finance when he brought down his balanced budget last year, which indicated that he had slashed left and right with his pencil, curtailing the expenditures of the Department of Public Works to the point they were in 1957-58, without any regard whatsoever to the effect upon the economy and without any regard to the necessity and desire of getting into the field of expansion of social capital investment.
This lack of planning appears again this year, indicating that we were in error last year in accepting the advice of the Minister of Finance, because the economic situation worsened rather than improved. We now find there is an expansion in the proposed expenditures of the Department of Public Works, which I suggest has been adopted to

Supply-Public Works
correct the situation. I suggest we should explore the activities of the Department of Public Works particularly with regard to the co-operation which exists, or does not exist, between that department and the other two levels of government. I suggest we should search for methods of attracting industry to depressed areas so as to bolster the economy as much as possible. We have entered this field to a limited extent by the creation of double depreciation, although I feel this will not in itself be sufficient. I agree with the statement contained in the report of the committee of that other place, which reads as follows:
The consequences of technological changes and the effects of declining industries are so large that little can be accomplished with marginal and small scale remedies.
This is what the Senate manpower employment committee said about the double depreciation effort of the government. In fact they made another reference, as follows:
Sporadic incursions into this problem and random flourishes are not going to bring results.
I think that is what we have with respect to this government and this department, sporadic incursions and random flourishes in all fields of activity in which this government engages, and the end result is not very beneficial to the economy or to respect for government or anything else. It breeds a degree of contempt for a government that has not the foresight to look past the end of its nose, and then when it suddenly discovers it has made an error it engages in an attempt to blacken the name of a public servant, as happened a few days ago, and lay all the blame on him.
I should now like to turn to the question of the trans-Canada highway, which comes under the Minister of Public Works also and which is in part a social capital investment. If my memory serves me, the original intention was to have the trans-Canada highway completed in 1956. By a subsequent change it was supposed to be completed by the end of December of last year. It is now expected that it will be completed by the end of December, 1963. In fact we have had three target dates for the completion of the trans-Canada highway. We have also had three or four different changes and increases in the amount of money which the federal government may contribute toward the construction of the trans-Canada highway. The amount has been increased from $150 million to $250 million and then to $350 million, and now I believe parliament has authorized that up to $400 million may be contributed toward the cost of the highway. We have also had an alteration in the formula from the original

50-50 basis to a 50-50 plus 90 per cent of 10 per cent of the mileage respecting the national parks.
The report of the trans-Canada highway for last year is a bit more cagily drawn up, and I imagine this reflects the attitude of the minister. In previous years the report was pretty definite and said that the highway would be completed by a certain time, and so on. I notice that the report is not quite that definite now, but speaks in terms of hopes and expectations for the coming year. I think this is more correctly aligned to the facts than the reports of previous years.
The trans-Canada highway itself, as should have been expected when it was originally conceived, has run into some formidable problems. One can build highways in the province of Saskatchewan much quicker and at much less cost than in some parts of British Columbia. I am sure a highway can be built in Manitoba at much less cost than along the rocky shores of Newfoundland, or in some parts of northern Ontario. All these different geographical conditions contributed greatly to the delays, postponements, extensions of time, increases in the amounts of money and changes in formula that were found necessary in order to complete the trans-Canada highway and make it a first-class coast to coast paved route.
In the four western provinces, with the exception of one part of British Columbia, we appear to be rushing toward the completion of the highway. On page 4 of the report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1960 some figures are given. I am sure these figures have changed since the publication of this report and the minister will undoubtedly indicate, or perhaps already has indicated in detail what the situation is in those provinces. I would point out that in the four provinces there is a total of-I had the total here, Mr. Chairman, but I cannot find it. In any event, of the total mileage in the four western provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, only 42 miles are indicated as not passable. There are 164 miles which are not paved and 152 of those are in British Columbia, the most notably difficult section being through the Rogers pass area.
The minister's predecessor, who is now the Secretary of State for External Affairs, when discussing this question a couple of years ago said in effect that it was not the intention of the government to abandon the contracts or agreements with respect to the trans-Canada highway once the highway had been completed. I read into that that it was at least the intention of the minister's predecessor to extend the present system or

agreements respecting the trans-Canada highway to other east-west highways. I hope this is still the situation so far as the present minister is concerned, because in northern British Columbia we-and when I say "we" I include everyone in the area, boards of trade, the unions, chambers of commerce, community associations and individuals alike- have been concerned with the development, building, completion and reconstruction of highway 16 and the extension of that highway eastward from Prince George to Jasper in Alberta, in order that we might have in that area an east-west access to our friends in the prairie provinces instead of having to go north to Fort St. John and Dawson Creek, although they are delightful places to visit, or south to some other part of the province.
If we are thinking in terms of this social capital and the need to engage in this sort of thing, now would be the time to do it; for if ever it was appropriate for the federal government to make overtures, as it were, or to get in touch with at least the four western provinces-and I mention those only because I am more familiar with them than I am with central Canada or the east in so far as highway building requirements are concerned- and indicate that the federal government is willing to participate financially with them in the construction of a so-called second trans-Canada highway, or a northern trans-Canada highway, running east-west along the general latitudes which cover Prince Rupert, Prince George and the like, this is the time.
There is one more reason for this, Mr. Chairman. It is not only the fact that we like to have fine black-top highways there, instead of gravel and earth highways and so on. There is also the question of our relationship with the United States and the state of Alaska, because they also are becoming more involved in tourism and in travel through their particular part of the country, and especially along highway 16 out to Prince Rupert. There is a possibility that within a year or a year and a half the Alaska government will build a so-called marine highway, or will build a number of ferries which will in fact carry automobiles and passengers to the ports of the Alaska Panhandle. Because the southern starting point of the service will be Prince Rupert, which is also the terminus of highway 16, I think it is most desirable that the federal government participate financially with respect to highway 16 as soon as possible. I should like the minister to indicate what is happening in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to be able to give the minister the time he deserves, but I only have five minutes to
Supply-Public Works
bring up two points that affect his department. I asked a question which was answered in the house on February 15, 1961, as found on page 2062 of Hansard. My question was:
How are the design contracts or awards given to architects by the Department of Public Works?
I should like the minister to note this question fairly closely, because I think I got a poor answer. The second part was:
Has the department received or noted any communications or views since 1957 which have been critical of the procedure in awarding commissions to architects?
This is the answer I received to these two questions:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to part 1 of the question is, on approval of the minister and authorization of treasury board. In answer to part 2, no such communications have been received by the department.
I want to draw the attention of the minister to a magazine that I would assume some of his senior officials would look at. It is the Canadian Architect. I think it is the main magazine in the field in Canada; and in the issue of December, 1960, there is an article entitled "Architecture's Big Clients". Then there is another article entitled "Five Years of Public Works". If they do not express views that are critical of the assignment of architects' commissions in the Department of Public Works, then I cannot read correctly. I should like to put one brief paragraph on the record to indicate the nature of the criticism. It reads as follows:
What is significant about this whole study is that the situation outlined in our April, 1957 issue, a relatively few architects receiving an extremely large proportion of the money that the Department of Public Works has to spend on architects' fees, continues to exist. We would certainly not press for D.P.W. jobs to be allotted right down the list of firms, alphabetically, one by one; nor do we deny that D.P.W. may well find it more convenient, or more satisfying, or more anything else, to work with one architect rather than another. We simply wonder if the department has really found the best way of awarding commissions, in view of the large amounts of public money it disburses and the fairly large number of competent architects who would like to do buildings for the government and are not doing so now.
All other considerations aside, a public building costing three or four million dollars or more is surely a proper subject for national or provincial competition. The department would certainly avoid a lot of criticism if such large commissions were awarded in this way; to our knowledge, only one of the 50 big buildings was so commissioned, and it was not built according to the winning design even then. We strongly recommend, therefore, that the department hold competitions for its big buildings, and we will continue to make this recommendation as long as the situation detailed here continues.
I do feel that those are certainly views that should have come to the attention of the department and the people in charge of architects' commissions. They certainly set

Supply-Public Works
up a criticism and give an analysis of which I would have thought the minister and the deputy minister would have been fully aware. I should like the minister to explain why this particular view was missed, and what reaction he and his officials have to these opinions expressed in what I understand is a reputable magazine. If it is, then I think this is a fairly serious criticism which should be answered.
The other point I want to bring to the attention of the minister is quite simple. I should like the assurance from him that the department is doing its best to police the fair wage section of the contracts that exist between it and its contractors. At the lake-head we have a higher wage level than other parts of the country because of the pulp and paper industry. When outside contractors bid on public works jobs in our part of the country, and they quite often do so, they are not prepared to pay the going rate in the area. I have found that the fair wage office of the Department of Labour has been remiss in keeping these matters up to date, and we have a succession of disputes and difficulties.
The other factor is that these contractors, because they cannot get tradesmen in our area to work for the rates they offer, bring in men from outside. Having regard to these two aspects of public works contracts, I should like the minister to explain to us just how they are policed and how much vigour is put into the policing of them. The word "police" may be unfortunate, but I think the minister knows what I mean.
As I said when I started, I regret that I cannot give the minister the attention I should like to give him. I wanted to deal with this loving article about him where he is rated as the scrappiest man in the cabinet. We have a sort of Jekyll and Hyde personality here. In Rosedale he is Uncle Dave, yet he says that here he finds it hard to control his bitter tongue. I assume that some time during the discussion of these estimates, Mr. Chairman, we will see something other than the Uncle Dave aspect.
