speechtext:
I should simply like to remark that the hon. member may have had some experience with bitter tongues during his encounter with Donald Gordon this morning in the railway committee.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m. 
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, the mood of the day appears to be more serene, and the minister has not opened the door to matters of the past, so I hope we will be able to discuss the present and the future without any interference.
Yesterday, I heard the minister state in his opening remarks that he expected the work to start soon on the new national library. I am very glad to hear it. Indeed, the need for it has been felt for some time. I realize that such things cannot be done overnight. Paris was not built in a day, nor will Ottawa.
A national library is a necessity in a capital city which has two universities. The students in those institutions need to have places where they can do research work and prepare for the future.
When I attended the University of Ottawa, students could go to the Carnegie library. Despite its limitations, this library was of great service, and enabled us to complete the subjects taught to us and even to learn things not included in the curriculum.
That is where I learned that under the French regime, in Canadian history, the greatest man who ever came to Canada from France was Jean Talon. Perhaps he did not have the glamour of Frontenac or Champlain, but he was a man of peace.
Moreover, he did not come to Canada to get rich in the fur trade. He came to build up a civilization and to ensure the welfare of his people.
He was the first to organize a great settlement scheme, and a great network of roads. It was thanks to his action that thriving communities sprung up between Quebec and Montreal.
This modest library, therefore, was of great benefit to us. The new national library will have an even greater impact because it will provide a means for more elaborate research.
We must not forget that in the final analysis, the purpose of a college education is to create personal working habits and to open up vistas in more than one field. Former students, having become adults, will find new sources of wisdom in this library.
Buildings erected in the vicinity of the parliament buildings should not detract from their style. There are several such buildings that we can admire, and they give Ottawa real architectural beauty.
This is also true of Quebec city, whose buildings are of a distinctive style.

In my view, the design of buildings in Ottawa should harmonize with the main building, namely the House of Commons. Their design should therefore reflect something of the past, and should not be too modern.
The customs building, on MacKenzie street, for instance, is rather attractive; the Chateau Laurier also fits in well with the parliament buildings.
Union station, however, is a monstrosity. If it is the intention to build something along those lines, let us at least hope it will be built away from the centre where it cannot be seen by visitors.
The confederation building, the justice building, the supreme court building, the veterans affairs and the trade and commerce buildings, are all very fine. As they are federal buildings, I hope that in co-operation with the national capital commission the Minister of Public Works will see to it that this style we like is continued.
However, in the building field, I note that there are about 15 projects which will be carried out within the coming years, and not a single one is to be erected on the Quebec side, in the district marked out for the national capital district. Yet, some buildings were erected miles away from the centre of the city, whereas, on the Quebec side, in Gatineau and Hull constituencies, there are marvellous sites very close to the center of the national capital and the parliament buildings which are not being used. Buildings need not necessarily be erected in my riding; there are excellent sites in Gatineau.
Part of the district is now being used as a national park. But there are other magnificent sites where federal buildings could be erected.
Why is construction of national buildings on the Quebec side being delayed? I do not, and cannot understand it. I hope the minister will try to discuss those things with national capital authorities and with the national capital commission, so that, in the immediate future, some sites might be found on the Quebec side for buildings worthy of our capital which is not limited to the city of Ottawa but comprises an area of about 30 miles. In that 30 mile area, there are possibilities for buildings which would indicate that we too are part of the Dominion of Canada, since our return of June 22, 1960.
I know that the minister has hardly mentioned the subject until now, because it is rather difficult, as there is no adequate bridge for people to cross over to our side of the river. But as the building of a new bridge has been decided, I hope that the minister will be encouraged to put up some new buildings there. Speaking of the bridge, we were 90205-6-407
Supply-Public Works
informed that agreements had been signed between the province of Ontario, the province of Quebec, the cities of Hull and Ottawa and the federal government. We also learned that engineers have been looking over the situation so as to pick the location and work out the cost of the bridge. But we have not heard anything since. I hope that the minister will be in a position to tell us, in his reply to various questions put to him, if all borings are completed, if the necessary engineering work is on the way, whether it is going to be a high-level or low-level bridge because, as I said in this house, if we are-and the day will come whether we like it or not-to dredge the Ottawa river as the Richelieu river is bound to be dredged, now is the time to plan for that.
No bridge is built for two days, 10 years or 20 years; it is a project which must last even for hundreds of years; then we might as well plan for it right now.
It could be argued that the other bridges are not high enough. Well, if we build another low-level bridge instead of having four or five bridges to raise, there will be five, six or seven.
As I said a while ago I asked for information about that and never got any answer. I hope that we shall be told whether this will be a high-level or a low-level bridge. If the decision is to be in favour of a low-level bridge, perhaps the minister could inform us whether the fact that the Ottawa river is bound to be dredged has been considered, and if so, perhaps he could tell us, in the event that a high-level bridge is to be built how this dredging can be done when we find that the only place where some kind of a harbour could be developed considering the ground level is Hull since the shore on the Ottawa side is too steep. We could also be told on what side the seaway should be extended to reach Deschenes lake, and then Rapide des Chats to continue up north to lake Timiskaming and finally to the French river.
We should be given that information, and if the department has not yet started any survey to that effect, I submit that the time has come to ask the engineers to set up an engineering commission, to look into the best method of deciding not only upon the type and site of the interprovincial bridge but also consider future bridges that are to be built as a result of this Ottawa river development which is bound to happen some day, in 10, 15 or 20 years from now, because no region such as this can be left undeveloped along the Ottawa river between the cities

Supply-Public Works
of Hull and Ottawa right down to the Montreal area, as long as it is possible to do so through industrialization which could supply work to thousands of people.
We should also like to know whether it would cost less to build a suspension bridge or whether it would be better to build one on piles. If the bridge is going to be on piles, we should be told to what depth they will be sunk. I have heard it said that on the Ottawa side, the first pile will have to be driven 125 feet below water level because there are 90 feet of water and about 30 feet of soft soil before reaching bedrock.
Those are things we could and should know. If the department has not yet started working on this I hope it will soon get going so that the house may be better informed.
One thing I should like to say about that bridge, is that we have been asking for it for quite a while. As early as 1955, I brought pressure to bear with the then minister of public works and he told me at the time that the bridge could not be built before the parties concerned gave their consent. The governments of Ontario and Quebec and the municipalities of Hull and Ottawa have exchanged correspondence for months, even years. One day, the Quebec premier said to me: If the federal government want bridges, let them build some themselves. In the face of such a negative attitude, it was difficult for us to proceed.
I then asked that the correspondence between the federal government and the government of the province of Quebec concerning the bridge be produced; my request was complied with on July 14, 1960. At the time, a letter which the city of Hull had sent to Mr. Diefenbaker on September 24, 1958, was produced. Then, a letter from Mr. Claude Gauthier, secretary to the Prime Minister, addressed to Mr. Leblanc, the Hull city clerk and dated October 1; a letter from mayor Thomas Moncion of Hull sent to Mr. Diefenbaker on January 19, was also tabled at that time; a letter dated February 6, 1959, in which Mr. Claude Gauthier, secretary, replied to mayor Moncion's letter. Then a letter dated March 18 which the Hull city clerk, Mr. Leblanc, sent to Mr. Diefenbaker on behalf of the municipality and with which he enclosed a resolution passed by the municipal council concerning the bridge. There is also the letter which secretary Claude Gauthier wrote to Mr. Leblanc on March 24, 1959, to acknowledge receipt of the resolution. And here is the letter which mayor Armand Turpin wrote to the Prime Minister on February 10, 1960, to stress once more the necessity and urgency of building such a bridge.

Here is another letter. On February 29, 1960, His Worship Mayor Turpin received a letter from the Prime Minister's office with regard to the communication he had sent.
On December 13, 1957, Mr. Young, deputy minister of public works, mentioned the possibility of extending Montclair boulevard and the Interprovincial bridge.
On February 10, 1960, there is another letter from Mr. Turpin. I am sorry, I note that it is a translation of a letter written in French by Mr. Turpin. The other documents are only translations.
And in all that correspondence, we find that Quebec authorities were not definitely against the project but did not seem overly interested.
Once again, I asked the minister for some information, which was supplied on April 27, 1961. Here again we have letters, especially one written by Mr. Winters in 1955.
The first motion for production of papers read as follows:
(Text):
A copy of all correspondence, telegrams, contracts, agreements and other documents exchanged between the federal government, the provincial governments of Quebec and Ontario, and the municipal governments of Hull and Ottawa since June 1, 1957, concerning the construction of a bridge over the Ottawa river between the cities of Hull and Ottawa.
(Translation):
The second motion for production of papers referred to-
(Text):
For a copy of all correspondence, telegrams, contracts, agreements and other documents exchanged between the federal government and the provincial government of Quebec, since November 15, 1955, concerning the construction of a bridge over the Ottawa river-
(Translation):
And there we have documents dating prior to the year 1957. As a matter of fact, there is a letter dated September 27, 1955, in which the then minister of public works, the Hon. Mr. Winters, invited the premier of Quebec, Mr. Duplessis, to come and discuss the building of a bridge. On September 30, the premier answered Mr. Winters that he hoped to be in Ottawa soon and to be able to discuss the matter with him.
On October 19, 1955, Mr. Winters wrote again to the Hon. Mr. Duplessis, asking him to meet with those primarily concerned with matter and more particularly with the Ontario premier and the Ottawa and Hull municipal authorities.

On October 31, 1955, Mr. Duplessis informed Mr. Winters by telegram that he had tried to phone him but without success, Mr. Winters being out of town. Mr. Duplessis was advising him he could not attend the meeting but that he would delegate a representative.
On November 10,	1955, the Hon. Mr. Winters sent a very long letter to Mr. Duplessis, giving him a detailed account of the action taken following discussions on the matter of the bridge with representatives of the province of Ontario and the cities of Ottawa and Hull.
On November 15, Mr. Duplessis replied to Mr. Winters thanking him for the information received and saying that he would consider the matter.
On January 13, 1957, Mr. Winters wrote a letter to Mr. Duplessis on all the points discussed since with those interested in the building of the bridge, briefing the premier on the situation.
On February 28, Mr. Winters wrote again to Mr. Duplessis:
(Text):
On November 10, 1956, I advised you that it was proposed to set up a committee to consider the matter of rearranging the approaches to the existing bridges between Ottawa and Hull, and the possible location of an additional bridge, as well as preliminary estimates of cost. An invitation was extended to you to have a representative on this committee.
The committee has now reported and, for your information, I am enclosing a copy of the minutes of their last meeting held December 14, 1956, as well as a copy of the consultant's report in which a recommendation is made for the construction of a new bridge.
I would welcome any comments you might care to make on this proposal.
Yours sincerely, Robert Winters.
(Translation):
On April 17, Mr. Winters wrote again to the Quebec premier. It was only on April 6, 1960, that a meeting was suggested, that the letter from the present Minister of Public Works was sent to Mr. Barrette who had then replaced Mr. Sauve as leader of the Quebec government; that was in April 1960. This is what the present Minister of Public Works said:
(Text):
My dear Premier:
I wish to refer to your letter of March 22 to Prime Minister Diefenbaker in regard to the above meeting.
I note with pleasure that representatives of the province of Quebec will attend.
I am also writing to the designated representatives of the province of Ontario and the mayors of Hull and Ottawa suggesting that the meeting be held in room 356-S of the House of Commons at 10.00 a.m., on Thursday, April 28, 1960.
Would you please let me know if this is agreeable to you.
(Translation):
And here we have letters and telegrams sent by the present Minister of Public Works 90205-6-407i

to convey his regrets for the delay in settling this problem. In fact, on April 22, 1960, the minister informed Antonio Barrette, premier of Quebec-
(Text):
Regret delay in replying to your letter of April eighth to Prime Minister. Would advise that two cabinet ministers from Ontario as well as mayors of Ottawa and Hull have indicated they will be present. Representation from your cabinet would be most welcome.
(Translation):
Here is another letter from the present Minister of Public Works to Antonio Barrette:
(Text):
On February 24, 1960, the following motion was passed in the House of Commons:
"For a copy of all correspondence, telegrams, contracts, agreements"-
(Translation):
It is about the motion for the production of papers which I have in hand now, asking for permission to make certain letters public.
Here is another letter of June 15, 1960. (Text):
Following your letter re producing correspondence Hull-Ottawa bridge. We have no objection to the production of this correspondence in the House of Commons.
(Translation):
On July 20, 1960, the present Minister of Public Works sent a letter to Mr. Rene Levesque, minister of public works in Quebec, informing him of the steps taken, mentioning the meetings that had taken place and asking him to continue the work already undertaken.
Then, the federal deputy minister of public works wrote Mr. Branchaud, chief engineer with the Quebec highway department, as follows:
(Text):
Reurtel meeting Ottawa-Hull inter provincial bridge will take place Thursday September eight ten a.m. room 238-S House of Commons Ottawa. This information was forwarded to the hon. Mr. Levesque in our letter July twenty as Quebec department of public works was only department represented at April meeting. Mr. Levesque was requested to advise if that time and date was satisfactory and also to forward names of those attending. Please advise-
(Translation):
Then there was another letter and a telegram sent by the present deputy minister to the Quebec minister of public works, Mr. Levesque.
Mr. Marc Picard sent a letter to the present deputy minister of public works:
(Text):
Department of Public Works. Sorry we did not find letter from hon. Walker re meeting Ottawa-Hull bridge for September. Agree meeting on September eight ten o'clock room 238-S House of Commons. Will be present hon. Rene Levesque minister of public works; Herve Gauvin, deputy minister; P. A. Dupuis, chief engineer, and myself. Marc Picard, technical adviser.

Supply-Public Works (Translation):
There we realize that things start moving. And the exchange of correspondence continues between the minister, the deputy minister and the provincial authorities. There is much activity, much action, because the urgency of that construction is realized.
When I asked for that correspondence and when it was produced, the minister said:
(Text):
While I am on my feet, Mr. Speaker, may I take this opportunity of adding that Quebec was brought into agreement for the first time on participation in the financing of the bridge by the government of former Premier Barrette.
(Translation):
Even though I looked through all the documents I had, which I had received from the Department of Public Works, I could not find a single letter, telegram or note to substantiate the minister's statement. The only two letters received from Mr. Barrette are the one I read a moment ago authorizing the production of the documents and this one, which was also addressed to the Prime Minister, like the first one, and which reads as follows:
(Text):
Pursuant to my letter dated the 22nd ultimo, I am pleased to inform you that Mr. C. R. Laberge, deputy minister of public works, and Mr. Georges Cote, director of surveys and cadastre services, department of lands and forests, will represent the province of Quebec at the conference to be held in Ottawa for the discussion of the project of a new bridge on the Outaouais river, between Ottawa and Hull.
If this conference should be at the ministerial level, I will delegate a member of the cabinet as my representative.
With my best personal regards, I remain- (Translation) :
And those two letters have been produced after the production of the other documents and not at the time of the first request, which goes back to July 14, 1960; and they had been sent to the Prime Minister in March and April 1960. I cannot understand why they have been added to those documents after their production. But the minister was wrong in saying that the premier of Quebec, Mr. Barrette, had been the first to agree to share financially in this project. I do not criticize Mr. Barrette for not having had the opportunity to do so during his tenure of office, for as soon as he became premier of Quebec, following many changes, it was logical to call an election.
But I cannot accept that he is the one who came to an agreement. Even if the minister says there was an agreement concluded over

the phone, that does not constitute an agreement to a financial sharing, because such agreements are not made over the phone. So, I suggest there must be a letter that could be shown to that effect.
I challenge the minister to produce one document which would prove that Premier Barrette was the first one to agree to share financially in the building of that bridge.
I am asking for the actual facts. I am asking for the tabling of documents which could prove that fact. But there is nothing to confirm that Premier Barrette had offered to share financially in the construction of that bridge. Such a statement saying that Premier Barrette was the first to agree to share financially in the construction of the bridge might mislead the population.
(Text):
-I take this opportunity of adding that Quebec was brought into agreement for the first time on participation in the financing of the bridge by the government of former Premier Barrette.
(Translation):
It does not exist. And if there was a telephone conversation note of it should have been taken in order to prove that it had taken place. We do not have to take the minister's or anybody else's word for it.
I have here the documents produced. These are the documents that we should have and I submit that the minister did not have the right to relate facts that I consider inaccurate since they are not borne out by the documents I asked for.
I hope, in spite of all that, that the minister will continue to step up things so that the interprovincial bridge be built before 1967, that is as early as possible, in two or three years maybe, so as to allow not only for a more complete development of the city of Hull, but also of Ottawa. Furthermore, it should be recognized that the bridge is urgently needed. I hope that the minister will shortly be able to give us better news than what we have been given so far.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to delay in any way the passage of the estimates of the Department of Public Works. However, I should not like to pass up this opportunity of expressing my appreciation to the minister and to his departmental officials. I must add that I can always count on an immediate, prompt and intelligent co-operation on the part of the minister and every member of his staff.
I thought I should take a few minutes of the time of the house to say a few words, because I want to put on record certain facts

of common knowledge that are at variance with the suggestions of hon. members opposite that nothing has been done in the Department of Public Works since the Conservative government came to power.
My hon. friend from Levis (Mr. Bourget) will certainly have a hard time convincing the people of the riding of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot that it has not been a good thing for them as well as for the rest of Canada to have a Conservative government in this country and, consequently a Conservative minister at the head of the Department of Public Works.
The only evidence I need in that respect is the speech just made by the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron), who tried for a halfhour to say that if the interprovincial bridge is built, it will not be thanks to the present Conservative government.
He repeated many times that all the efforts which were made until now to bring about the construction of a bridge between Hull and Ottawa, had led nowhere-

I do not make it a habit of trying to contradict the hon. member when he speaks. However, I never said the Conservative government had done nothing because, in fact, the government started the work. I simply stated that the minister had no right to say that it was Mr. Barrette who had been the first to reach an agreement. That is all I said.

Mr. Chairman, when the hon. member for Hull had the floor, a while ago, and was saying that the minister had lied, I came very close to getting up but I have shown him the courtesy that he claims he has for others and I remained silent.
But I think he had no right to state a few minutes ago that the minister was wrong in saying that the premier of Quebec, Mr. Barrette, was the one who had brought the negotiations to a head on this matter.
The country at large and in particular the province of Quebec are quite aware of that fact, which seems to be unknown to the hon. member for Hull.
At the next election, the people of Hull will consider the situation in its proper light and we shall see what will happen.
I refer again, Mr. Chairman, to remarks made by the hon. member for Levis who said it had not been a good thing for my riding to have in the house a Conservative representative since June 10, 1957.
Supply-Public Works
That is a surprising statement coming from the hon. member for Levis, who is himself an engineer and who moreover was the parliamentary assistant to the minister of public works under the former administration.
In the St. Hyacinthe-Bagot riding, retaining walls had been built along the Richelieu and Yamaska river. In St. Charles on the Richelieu, from 1936 to 1957, that is under the 21-year Liberal administration, a wall 2,381 feet long, costing $58,806, was built.
Friends of the former government must have had properties in the area.

Quite probably. In St. Denis, a retaining wall 2,207 feet long was built at a cost of $44,487. In St. Joseph, $3,443 was spent on a wall 250 feet long.
I am coming now to the years 1958, 1959 and 1960. Let us see what the Tory party did in three years for the St. Hyacinthe-Bagot riding: St. Charles, at a cost of $54,582, retaining walls over a distance of 1,577 feet. At St. Denis, the expenditure was $83,467, for retaining walls 3,416 feet long.
At St. Joseph, $77,082 was spent on retaining walls 2,500 feet long.
For this year 1961, appropriations by the Department of Public Works amount to $110,000 for St. Charles and to $143,000 for the village of St. Denis.
Mr. Chairman, if you add up all those amounts, you get, after 21 years of Liberal administration, a total distance of 4,838 feet and a total value of $106,036 of retaining walls erected on shores damaged by navigation.
During the last three years, that is since the Conservative party took over, retaining walls have been built in my riding over a distance of 15,933 feet at a total cost of $469,131. I need not point out that those projects have provided employment for my constituents.
For all his long-winded statements, declamations and rantings, the hon. member for Levis will not succeed in making the people of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot believe that the present member did not obtain for his constituency more than the former Liberal regime, palsied by inertia, ever provide for his county.
In the matter of federal buildings, Mr. Chairman, thanks to the co-operation of the

Supply-Public Works
present Minister of Public Works, my constituency has obtained two post offices, one in the village of St. Germain of Graham and the other in St. Pie.
Furthermore, preparations are about to be completed for the construction of a federal building in St. Hyacinthe, which will house the federal services of the constituency of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot.
Since the beginning of the century, there has not been any federal construction in that constituency.
The election of a Conservative government led by a prime minister with foresight who has the welfare of the nation at heart was needed before my riding obtained what it needed.
Mr. Chairman, I would now like to talk about a matter which does not come directly under the department whose estimates we are now discussing. And I do not talk about the forthcoming construction of a tunnel.
Mr. Chairman, since I want to save you the trouble of calling me to order, I will immediately ask the Minister of Public Works for another post office building in St. Damase an up-and-coming parish of my constituency. The local farm and poultry co-operatives have an excellent reputation and are a credit to the industrious and clever spirit of our people.
According to the Postmaster General, postal revenue in that place exceeds $3,000 and I believe that the good people of St. Damase fully deserve a new post office.
I also want to deal for a few minutes with the activities of the present Conservative government in the field of housing. Mr. Chairman, it is a known fact that since the Conservative government came to power, it has set itself to improve the National Housing Act. Under the Liberal administration, when an individual wanted to build a house, the maximum loan available to him was only $12,800, while today it is $14,200. Here again, the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget) will be hard put to convince the Quebec people that the coming to power of a Conservative government was not a happy event.
I should also like to call the minister's attention to the trans-Canada highway and to ask his co-operation in this regard. At the present time, plans are under way in my riding with respect to a section of the trans-Canada highway. The new route planned

by the Quebec government will bring about an unfortunate situation; in fact, the best ancestral lands in my riding will be cut up.
Last week end, some farmers came to see me and urged me to use my influence in order to convince the proper authorities to spare their farms, both in the main concession of La Presentation parish, and in one concession of St. Thomas d'Aquin parish.
If the present plans of the Quebec Liberal government are carried out, it will be disastrous, because the best farm lands of my riding will be cut in two.
Mr. Chairman, men and women, dedicated farmers, and God knows there are none to spare in Quebec, have urged me in a sobbing voice to make representations on their behalf.
I therefore urge the Minister of Public Works to try and convince the Quebec minister of highways to spare that part of my riding which is the most beautiful and the most productive, and to please adopt the former proposed route.
Mr. Chairman, as member for the riding of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot, it is my duty to sound the alarm. If this project for highway No. 9 through the St. Hyacinthe riding is carried out, it will be a disaster. For years to come, these farmers will bitterly regret having abandoned their land under such intransigence and misunderstanding. And, once again, Mr. Chairman, I urge the Minister of Public Works to be good enough to bring the Quebec highway minister to reason, to kindly save this lovely part of the Quebec garden which includes the lands of the main concession of La Presentation parish and also other concessions in St. Thomas d'Aquin parish.
We are going to build elevated highways just to please you.

No, there are other methods available.
I would not want to resume my seat, Mr. Chairman, without saying a few words about the awarding of contracts. A well established policy in the department is to call for public tenders. I have no complaint about that. I think public funds should be spent in the best interest of Canadians. But matters are going a bit too far, because of the ignorance of some caretakers.
In the town of St. Hyacinthe, in my riding, two or three plumbers were asked to tender for repairs amounting to $10, $12 or

$15. Now, not a single hon. member who is intelligent and has his own interests at heart would bother three or four contractors and ask them to bid for so measly an amount. People in charge should have the latitude to make their own decision and ask a particular contractor to do the work.
I would also ask the minister to consider the possibility of limiting calls for tenders on contracts for $25,000 or less to contractors in the constituency. In each constituency there are qualified contractors who can properly undertake any kind of contract for plumbing, joinery, heating or electricity, required by the department. I am saying this in all frankness, it is most annoying for a taxpayer, who pays taxes to the town and contributes to the economic life of the community, that contractors 100, 125 or even 200 miles away be invariably awarded contracts which actually should have been awarded to local residents.
Therefore, I ask the minister not to follow the example of the government of the province of Quebec and enact legislation restricting all contracts for amounts of $25,000 or less to political supporters who are invited to bid. What I am asking is that those contracts of $25,000 or less be restricted to local contractors and that they be awarded following a public call for tenders.
Mr. Chairman, I would not want us to commit the same sins as the present Quebec government. After claiming throughout the last electoral campaign that there would no longer be any patronage, they are the very ones who, more than ever, have introduced patronage in the province of Quebec. I am only asking the minister to reserve to contractors of ridings concerned contracts for $25,000, or less. I am not asking the minister to follow the example of the Quebec department and to award those contracts to selected contractors, friends of the party. I do not want that, because I do not believe it is in the best interests of the people. What I ask is that those contracts be restricted to contractors of the constituency. I feel quite at ease to say here that, in my constituency and in the ridings of my hon. friends here, there are honest and qualified contractors who can do the work which the Department of Public Works wishes to have carried out.
Before I resume my seat, Mr. Chairman, I should like to repeat that, even if he raises his voice, the hon. member for Levis will
Supply-Public Works
not succeed in making the people of the province of Quebec forget that in 1946-47, the Liberals spent $147.5 million for public works whereas, the Conservatives have earmarked $220 million for public works this year.
Nor will the hon. member for Hull convince the people that he does not have the fullest confidence in the ability of the present Minister of Public Works when he gets down on his knees to recommend that the interprovincial bridge be built as soon as possible.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the most eloquent testimonial of the unlimited confidence the Liberals have in the present Conservative government. The latter will certainly prove them right in the future.

speechtext: Shall vote 329 carry?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words before this vote carries. One thing we have appreciated about the minister is his refreshing candor. I can remember last fall when we waited in vain to hear what the government was going to do about unemployment. We were very surprised when nothing appeared in the speech from the throne.
Then we listened to speech after speech claiming there was no unemployment. Finally, this minister made a speech on the radio on the program "The Nation's Business" in which he admitted there was unemployment. He admitted there was a serious problem and it would take a while for us to solve this problem. If we have no reason for being appreciative of anything else that this hon. gentleman has done, I think those of us on this side of the house have cause to be appreciative of this moment of truth which seemingly came to the Minister of Public Works although it failed to come to his colleagues. For that reason, we tend to forgive him when sometimes in the house he uses two lines of argument which seem to conflict as has been indicated by the fact that he stands up and, with what we regard as a refreshing flourish, once again reads out the number of housing starts for the last month. Then, he tells us what a wonderful thing this is because it is providing more employment. Then he turns around and tells us that, really public works do not provide very much employment, and public works will not solve the unemployment problem.

Supply-Public Works
We believe that down in his heart he knows that public works do provide a great deal of employment in the long run. They have the general effect of increasing the social capital. They have the long term effect of increasing the impetus toward a healthy economy in other sectors as well as the public sector. In his own heart, he knows that a really dynamic program of low cost housing subsidized by the federal government would do a great deal toward solving unemployment.
I think he knows that if the dominion bureau of statistics tells us we are going to need 10 major universities in the next 10 years, if these were constructed by his administration that would do a great deal to help unemployment. I think this minister will undoubtedly claim that I am being very unrealistic. However, this morning the Prime Minister said that the government is going to do something about the athletic achievements of the youth of this nation. If the Minister of Public Works embarked upon a program of building recreational centres across this country, that too would aid in reducing unemployment. It is for this reason we, in this corner, have a great deal of respect for this hon. gentleman, even though he sometimes astonishes us by suggesting he really cannot do very much about unemployment except provide a few pick and shovel jobs once in a while. I believe the minister feels that if he were given the opportunity he could devise an imaginative, ingenious, dynamic program, and that is what we are hoping to see.
In so far as the local scene is concerned I am afraid I cannot, at this time, put forward any suggestions that the minister might take home with him to think over during the week end. I should like to say we have one or two very interesting new federal buildings. The one federal building which houses the post office, as well as other offices, is one of the most attractive buildings in the community. However, when they built the unemployment insurance offices they constructed perhaps the ugliest building in the community, which is unfortunate. I believe. that this building has had a tremendous amount of use, but the same level of architectural excellence was not achieved that was the case with the post office building. My colleague suggests that it is the ugliest and the busiest building.
However, we hope that we will soon see the minister letting quite a few contracts in my area. We understand we are to have
an airport, and although I realize this does not come within his jurisdiction, nevertheless we expect to see some action being taken by the public works department in that area.
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister one or two problems that have been brought to my attention by the people of my constituency. One of them is really a repetition of a subject referred to by the hon. member for Nipissing, and that is finding a means of providing N.HA. mortgages for older houses. I have spoken about this to the minister in private, and other people have spoken to me about it. I feel that we have drowned ourselves in a program of construction of two and three bedroom bungalows. We are wallowing in these bungalows. We need now a more diversified approach to the whole problem of housing. After the war a great many young families bought these bungalows, and they now want larger homes. Because of the difficulty of financing them, they are unable to obtain these homes. I feel such action would have a tremendous effect upon the economy as a whole if the minister could find some way of solving this problem.
I realize that this is a distinct problem. I realize there is a problem of priority. I realize a problem is presented by the fact that people might use these mortgages in a way in which they would be using national funds for purposes which even we in this corner would find it hard to justify. However, I believe the minister has the ingenuity to get around these things. Perhaps we could take a tip from the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Let us set up some method of screening people in order to determine what the use of these mortgages will be, and only give mortgages to people who have a real justification. I am sure that with the amount of energy the minister has displayed in the past he can get around this difficulty. I am hoping that very soon we will see a dynamic answer to this problem of mortgages for older homes, so that we can get these larger familities who are now in bungalows moved into the older, larger homes without virtually bankrupting themselves by so doing.
The second problem which I have mentioned, but which I should like to go over once again, is this matter of land assembly. We, in Peterborough, have more land assembly areas than any other community in Canada. I should like to commend the minister and his department upon what has been achieved in connection with these land assembly projects. We need more of them so that we can give cheap land to people who want to build houses. However, I am going to suggest that we need greater federal control over these projects. We have people buying land under

the land assembly system and they put up houses which could not, even by the greatest stretch of the imagination, be called low cost houses.
The land assembly idea-that is the dominion, provincial and municipal governments going together and buying up a large amount of land, then selling it virtually at cost to people-is a first class example of democracy at work. I believe this was the original concept. However, I wish there could be a little more control over it so that the people who really need low cost housing can gain through the land assembly system, and not have larger, more luxurious homes being placed upon this land to the detriment of the people who want to put up low cost houses.
There are a great many interesting items under this minister's control. One is fire prevention. I notice that this minister is giving $5,000 to the Canadian joint fire prevention publicity committee. This is an area which I think needs a great deal of attention. I am sure that when this item is called there will be a great many members who will have something to say about it.
Another item of interest is housing research and community planning. This, too, will require some discussion. This is one of the major areas to which we in Canada need to devote our energies. What kind of communities do we want? What kind of planning do we need? Many visitors come to our country and say our communities not only lack character but they lack any form, any planning whatever. I think this is something on which we should now get busy very quickly. I hope this item is going to be sufficient to provide the kind of planning which is necessary in these communities all across Canada.
I believe this minister has a tremendous opportunity to make this country a better place in which to live, and I am sure he is going to accept that challenge.

Mr. Chairman, before asking for additional public works for my riding, I should like the minister to know that I am not ungrateful for the work which has been done, and which is in the process of being done in my constituency. I am particularly pleased that a decision has been reached to reconstruct the wharf at Botwood. The reconstruction of this wharf will fill a long felt need in this important shipping port. The wharf at Goose Bay is nearing completion. Other projects scheduled for this year at Jackson's Arm, Harry's Harbour, L'Anse au Clair and L'Anse au Loup are jobs which need to be done. Progress is being made on the new Canadian National dock at Lewisporte. But while I am indeed grateful for the work 90205-6-408
Supply-Public Works
which is being done in my riding, I feel that I must point out the need for additional public works in Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador, with its long sea coast and its maritime activities. I should like to speak particularly about Labrador.
As I have had said previously in this chamber, and I hope hon. members will bear with me if I repeat it, Labrador is an extremely important source of fishery products today, and its importance is increasing all the time as more and more of the fish plants in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia depend upon fish caught in Labrador waters. Not only is Labrador important to the province of Newfoundland and to the economy of the whole of the Atlantic provinces but it is, of course, of the greatest importance to those people who live in the villages along its coast. It is a well known fact that small marine works encourage the fisheries. Small marine works such as small wharfs and breakwaters permit the fishermen to operate when otherwise they could not do so. These works extend the period of the fishing season and the benefit which accrues to the fishermen and to the economy as a whole is far beyond the small amount of money it takes to provide these small public works.
Some work has been done on the Labrador coast but I would request more attention for these small communities along the coast of Labrador and more of these marine works which will make it easier and more practical for those who live in these fishing communities to carry on their avocations. A number of additional works are needed. I will not attempt to list them all. From time to time I have written to the minister's department with regard to them. However, I think of the coastal villages of Makkovik, Square Islands, Georges Cove, Capstan Island and others where the need for wharves or community stages or both exist and where an investment in small marine works will unquestionably bring real dividends. The waters of Labrador are extremely productive and there is no doubt that these marine works will enable the productivity of these places to be increased. I would ask that the minister give careful and sympathetic consideration to increasing the amount of money spent in Labrador.
In northern Newfoundland some dredging is required at St. Anthony, Goose Cove and Englee. A wharf at Roddickton which was partly reconstructed needs to be completed. A wharf for Goose Cove should be considered and wharves for Miles Cove and other places in Green bay. There are also other places where the need for marine work is equally acute. I would express the hope that northern Newfoundland, Labrador and the rest of that

Supply-Public Works
part of the coast of Newfoundland included in my riding would be given sympathetic and careful attention by the Minister of Public Works. A small dredging operation is required at Lewisporte at Mussel bay where an expenditure that may be more than a few hundred dollars would reduce the distance which the fishermen are obliged to go in order to discharge their products.
I mentioned earlier that the cost of some of these projects is low compared with the service that they render. In that connection I think of a small job that was done at Shoe Cove last year which cost very little. A small breakwater which consisted mainly of filling up with concrete a gap between two rocks has made it infinitely easier for the fishermen of Shoe Cove to carry out their operations. There are many places like that where comparatively small expenditures result in making fishing ports of much greater use to the fishermen and, in the long run, enabling them to increase their catch and the total production of fish.
With respect to community stages may I say this. Although I mentioned this matter on the estimates of the Minister of Fisheries, as the Department of Public Works builds them I think it proper that I should make some reference to them here. The program of building community stages undertaken by the federal Department of Fisheries and Department of Public Works has more than justified the decision to build them. These community stages are of inestimable value to the fishing settlements in which they have been built. They provide premises from which to fish and places in which to handle gear. They bring fishermen together so that they can deal more effectively as groups rather than as individuals. By and large they have given a considerable impetus to the fisheries.
I might add here that, in my opinion, in a country such as ours with a growing population, not only should new industries be developed but old ones should be expanded. There is no doubt in my mind that the community stages program resulted in an expansion of the fishing business and that they will continue to be used more and more as time goes on. I would express a sincere hope that this program will be continued and that a community stage program will be planned to be carried on year after year until all the communities which require them have been supplied with them. There is nothing of greater importance in the whole program of public works than is the building of these community stages. Again they provide an instance in which comparatively small amounts of money provide really great and worth-while returns.
Since the last estimates of the Minister of Public Works were before the committee for consideration, two small post office buildings have been erected in Glenwood and Norris Arm in my riding. They fill a need which has been acute for a long time. I wish to mention here that I should like to see a number of these small buildings erected in my riding. I would mention again the need for a post office building in Happy Valley in Labrador, a community which has needed such a building for a long time and in which the need now is greater perhaps than it ever was. I would hope that before the year is out some action would be taken to provide a public building for the community of Happy Valley. I would also revert to the need for dredging in northern Newfoundland. I have every reason to believe that this matter is under review by the department and I would express the hope that a favourable decision will be arrived at.
One of the great requirements of the province of Newfoundland is the completion of the trans-Canada highway. A large section of the trans-Canada highway passes through my district and the completion of this highway is placing a very great strain upon the finances of the province. In view of the fact that Newfoundland and the Atlantic provinces in general have a severe transportation handicap by the very nature of their geographical position, I suggest that it would be only fair for the Department of Public Works to build at their cost, or to undertake the major part of the cost of completing the trans-Canada highway in the Atlantic provinces.
The completion of the trans-Canada highway by the federal Department of Public Works, or the greater part of the cost of it being paid by the federal government would provide something in the way of compensation for transportation handicaps in that area. It seems to me this would permit the provincial governments concerned to devote more funds to building secondary roads in remote areas. This aspect of the completion of the trans-Canada highway is one which I have mentioned before. I hope the idea has not been lost sight of by those who have charge of the trans-Canada highway program.
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, those who live in the more fortunate and wealthier parts of Canada cannot properly appreciate the great need for additional transportation facilities in places where these facilities are somewhat restricted. At the same time it may be difficult for those living in central Canada to realize the great value and the utterly vital importance of small marine

works to the economy of coastal towns and villages. But these needs are very real in the Atlantic provinces.
These needs are very evident to everyone who lives in my riding, which includes a great northern area. When the minister and his officials sit down to make up their estimates in regard to what should be done during the coming year all over this vast area of Canada, I would like them to bear in mind that considering the value of some of these works, the cost in dollars and cents is actually very small. The cost of a wharf or a small breakwater is very small indeed compared with the utility it gives, compared with the increase in production which it makes possible and the increased standard of living which results.
I would ask again that the Minister of Public Works and his officials keep in mind the relative importance of these small marine works, remembering that where a small wharf is built it enables the fishery to carry on when otherwise perhaps it would not be possible to carry on and that it has been proven that where these works have been allowed to disappear, the returns to the fishermen have fallen off. I would ask the minister and his officials to keep in mind that the real, economic advantages and the improvement to living standards brought about by these small works are away beyond the relatively small cost involved.

Mr. Chairman, there are a few brief remarks I should like to make at this stage of the estimates of the Department of Public Works. First of all I should like to congratulate the minister and thank the departmental officials for the consideration which has been given to northern Manitoba in the form of post offices, alterations and improvements to federal buildings, and particularly in C.M.H.C. housing loans, which up until this time we have encountered some difficulty in procuring for that area. Things have been improving immensely over the past year and a half and many of the areas are now receiving the benefits of central mortgage and housing loans. I should also like to thank the department for the consideration they have given northern Manitoba in the construction of many small docks and wharves.
However, my prime purpose in speaking on this particular subject today results from some very disturbing news items which have appeared in Manitoba newspapers these past few days. Articles have appeared in the Winnipeg newspapers and in the Manitoba weeklies which have resulted, apparently, from a visit to northern Manitoba of the 90205-6-408i
Supply-Public Works
newly elected leader of the Liberal party in Manitoba, Mr. Gildas Molgat.
Although I must say there are some aspects of Mr. Molgat's report with which I agree, I do take violent exception to others which in my opinion leave the inference that nothing whatsoever has been done in respect to the very important projects and problems which exist at Churchill, Manitoba. According to a report contained in the Winnipeg Free Press of June 13, upon his return to Winnipeg Mr. Molgat reported:
The government has frozen the sale of all new lots in town for the past two years while provincial and federal authorities carry out studies on the planned move.
That is, the planned move of the town. The article continues:
Word of the impending action was brought to Winnipeg Tuesday by provincial Liberal leader Gildas Molgat, who has just returned from a tour of the north. Mr. Molgat said he plans to raise the issue at the special summer session of the legislature.
That is, the Manitoba legislature. For Mr. Molgat's information, and wishing him all success in any assistance he may be able to give in solving the problems of Churchill, I would like to say that this will definitely not be the first time, if he raises the matter in the Manitoba legislature, that the problem has been raised there. I wish to assure him that both this federal government and the present government of Manitoba have been working in co-operation over the past three to three and one half years on this particular problem. Mr. Molgat says that the situation at Churchill is an intolerable one at this time. That is one of the points with which I agree. The situation is very bad and I sincerely hope that something can be done about it in the near future.
However, I do believe that the article leaves the impression with the people of Manitoba that nothing is being done and that the recommendations have been pushed under the rug. That is not the case, and I should like to state to the committee at this time that Mr. Molgat is specifically referring to a situation which is being studied, and that is, whether the town should be relocated or redeveloped at its present site. I suggest that Mr. Molgat has failed to report to the people of Manitoba in regard to the assistance which has been forthcoming for the past four years.
I can recall when I first went to Churchill to find out what the people's complaints were in that area that there were three or four specific problems involved. Those problems primarily were in respect to the establishment of a sewer and water system, adequate power supply, and the hard surfacing of the road to the army camp. They also wanted to have a new water supply system. For the

Supply-Public Works
benefit of Mr. Molgat and those individuals who are interested I should like to place on the record at this time the statement that, due to the co-operation between the provincial and federal governments, some of these projects-in fact most of them-have already been accomplished, yet I cannot forget the fact that there is one very serious problem in that area.
A new water system, which has been the subject of requests on the part of that town for many years, is now under construction and should be in operation within a few months, at least by the end of this year. Incidentally, the cost of that new water supply system, which will benefit not only the army camp, the national harbours board and other federal government establishments and the town itself, is in the neighbourhood of $967,000. This project is being carried out under an arrangement between Department of Public Works, and the Department of National Defence.
One of the other projects of interest to the people of Churchill, as expressed at the time I first visited the town, had reference to their increasing power requirements. At that time the townsite was being supplied power by the national harbours board. However, the national harbours board unfortunately could not supply sufficient power to meet the requirements of the town. Through an arrangement made with the Manitoba power commission, in which the government of Manitoba, as well as the Department of National Defence played a large part, an arrangement was agreed upon under which anyone in the Churchill townsite area using power is now able to get sufficient power at a greatly reduced rate, compared with what was previously being paid.
The people also asked to have the road to the army camp hard surfaced. Last fall this road was hard surfaced between Fort Churchill and the townsite at a cost of approximately $135,000.
I realize that this particular problem regarding the final decision as to whether the townsite is going to be relocated or re-veloped at its present site is of great importance to the people of Churchill at this time. Mr. Molgat's report gave me the impression that he felt nothing was being done at Churchill but I should also say that additional wharfage is being constructed at the port of Churchill at the present time at an expenditure of something over $5 million. That is another project which the people of that area have been requesting for many years.
Mr. Molgat has criticized both the provincial and the federal governments for the length of time that has been taken to complete

a study in regard to the town. I have on many occasions felt that this study was taking a great deal of time. I know that it is hoped and anticipated that this very necessary study will be completed before the end of this year at which time, I feel quite certain, both the provincial and federal governments will be in a position to meet and agree in regard to the possibility of servicing a new townsite, if that is the decision, or putting services in at the present site.
It is my understanding that the first part of the report of that study, which is now being conducted, indicates the desirability of relocating the townsite at a site approximately five miles from the present townsite. If that desirability is borne out by further study I am quite sure that the work which is being carried out by the two governments concerned will be realized and that an arrangement can be made to provide the necessary services for the people of Churchill.
As I have said, I agree with some portions of Mr. Molgat's report of his visit to Churchill, particularly that portion regarding the extreme necessity for action being taken at the earliest possible moment. However, I very definitely feel that both governments are at this time doing everything within their power. It is my hope that the study will be completed as quickly as possible and that the two governments concerned will arrive at an early agreement.
Mr. Chairman, before resuming my seat I should like to refer to one other project for northern Manitoba. I would respectfully request the minister to give consideration at the earliest opportunity to the desire and necessity of federal buildings being located at the new townsite of Thompson. This town is growing very rapidly and I am sure that the departments of this government will require office space in the area, so I again ask the minister to consider the possibility of building a federal government building there.
He knew it a couple of days later.

He knew it when he made the statement. I knew that by the look on his countenance, the sardonic look in his eye and the curl of his lips. But, Mr. Chairman, about three and a half weeks later the by-election was held. May I tell the Minister of Public Works that his statement was used by the Conservative supporters of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. The gentleman to whom the minister referred in his answer on May 4 has been returned and is now the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich in this house by the grace of a majority of just over 500.
The Minister of Public Works should make it clear to the committee whether the statement he made prior to the by-election was just a bribe, a political statement, or whether, it having paid off, something is going to be done about the reeve and about the construction of that breakwater. It does not appear in the estimates this year. This may be understandable because I presume they were printed-they must have been-prior to May 4. Since no mention of it is made in the estimates, I think we can rightfully ask the minister whether there is to be a supplementary estimate brought down for the construction of this breakwater. The minister owes it to the people of Esquimalt-Saanich, to the people of British Columbia and to this House of Commons to assure us that the statement made on May 4 was not just made for the purposes of the by-election. The minister ought to tell us that he is going to follow through with it and that we shall have a statement from him either now or when we reach the particular item on whether construction is to proceed. If it does not proceed, then the minister stands guilty of bribery through using his office for by-election purposes. I would not want the minister to be criticized nor condemned in that way. This is the only reason why I remind him of the brief he received in April and the statement he made on May 4. I realize that if we wait until we get to the specific item we sometimes get this answer, "Why did you not let me know about this before; it may take a little while to find the answer?"

Supply-Public Works
There is one other matter that I should like to draw to the minister's attention at this time in the hope that either now or when we get to the item dealing with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation he will comment on the matter that I shall now deal with. I was quite disturbed when a few months ago I was told by contracting firms in the construction industry that they were almost at a complete loss to know what were the actual requirements as to housing standards for construction coming under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. They told me that it is practically impossible for anybody in the construction industry to know what are the minimum required housing .standards.
I was so intrigued by that information that several weeks ago I wrote a letter to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation asking them to let me have their regulations concerning housing standards. I appreciate the fact that they sent me the information I requested by return mail. I hold in my hand now a document entitled "Housing Standards", which gives the minimum requirements for plans, construction and materials in respect of detached and semi-detached houses, duplex and semi-detached duplex houses and row housing. The date of issue is January, 1958. This document, which sets forth the minimum standards for housing, is some 116 pages long.
I can understand why it takes 116 pages to set forth the minimum C.M.H.C. housing standards as outlined for them by the division of building research of the national research council. But I draw to your attention, Mr. Chairman, the fact that this 116-page document has been amended three times without consolidation. I also have in my hand what is termed amendment No. 1. It is a 7-page document amending the original document to which I referred a few moments ago. I also have here amendment No. 2. This is a 16-page document amending amendment No. 1 and also amending the original document on minimum standards. I also have here amendment No. 3 which is 24 pages long. It amends amendment No. 2, amendment No. 1 and the original document. Section after section is amended which means that you have to tie them together, and I can certainly understand why many firms in the construction industry have told me that they defy anyone in the industry and the inspectors of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to tell them exactly what the rules and regulations are with respect to minimum standards under C.M.H.C. There are 47 pages of amendments to amendments to amendments to the original document. Just how inefficient can people be?

I want to be absolutely honest. I understand that for months Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been working on a revision and consolidation for the purpose of producing a new book on housing standards. I cannot quite understand why it takes months to do that. I understand further that the book is not ready yet for the printers and the industry.
As the minister knows, I was in the construction industry for many years so that I think I know whereof I speak to quite an extent so far as construction is concerned. I am most disturbed by some of the reports now being circulated as to changes being contemplated in the new revision. It has come to my attention that there are suggestions with respect to lowering the standards of construction of housing built under the National Housing Act. From information that has come to my attention I know that consideration is being given to the lowering of the quality of lumber by one grade. I know that the widening of the distance between beams and joists is under consideration.
I want to draw to the attention of the minister the need of a consolidation of the minimum standards so that not only contractors but the corporation's own inspectors will understand what the minimum standards are. In addition, to my mind it is of the utmost importance that there should be no lowering of standards in the new revision. We want to have homes that will not deteriorate to a considerable extent after a few years. In certain circumstances lowering the quality of the lumber by one grade is not good and widening the centre to centre distance between joists and beams is also not good. I believe that those recommendations were made by the construction association. I hope the minister will not allow building standards to deteriorate.
Because of the terms of the act under which the mortgage is repaid over a period of 25 or 30 years before people can own their homes, I hope that in the interests of good housing construction standards will be maintained, that the quality of lumber will be maintained and the distance between joists, beams or studs will be properly maintained. I sincerely hope that now or when the specific vote is under discussion the minister will tell us what is being done about the consolidation of the regulations and the maintenance of standards for the well-being of future home owners.
Does the minister want to speak?
