The following day, in the absence of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan), the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) replied as follows:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for St. Ann asked whether I was aware of certain comments of the chairman of the board of directors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation with respect to the search for a suitable location in the city of Montreal where C.B.C. operations will be consolidated. I did notice this report, and I am informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that a final decision has not been taken with respect to the location described in the question, as both the city and the corporation have decided to study one or more additional locations before deciding on the matter.
What most surprised me when I heard the minister's statement, Mr. Chairman, was that in February 1960, after a serious study had been made of the situation, the C.B.C. had accepted this location in principle. This was over 18 months ago, and now the C.B.C. is considering whether it really should locate in this area. If government officials are that slow in reaching a decision, how can you expect this organization to function properly?
Every aspect of this location has been thoroughly considered, and the city is prepared to expropriate, but now everything is held up by the C.B.C.'s inability to reach a decision. I therefore ask the government, through the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), to tell us yes or no whether it intends to accept the land made available to the C.B.C.
In the affirmative, the municipal authorities will be encouraged to build houses elsewhere for the displaced people, not to mention the fact that this will improve this section of Montreal. In the negative, then a new study should be made to find the best way to deal with the situation. Such a study should not be allowed to go on indefinitely, as this would slow down the development of that section.
I would also ask the minister, in considering requests from any administration, whether it would be possible to eliminate all the red tape, because it can hold up action indefinitely, as in the case of the C.B.C. scheme, which has come to nothing after 18 months, despite the fact that an agreement had practically been reached at the time.
It seems to me that the various departments of government should be more diligent and speed up the examination of petitions from municipal governments. For instance, a petition from the city of Montreal concerning a new construction project on the boulevard des Trinitaires in the west section

of Montreal, must have reached the minister's desk by now. At present, the land is vacant and belongs to the city. All that is needed is the approval of both the provincial and federal governments before a housing project is started there consisting of 250 to 300 housing units. If that project is carried out, the city will then participate in another project whereby people could be provided with living accommodation.
What I mean, Mr. Chairman, is that the government should not delay in replying to municipalities in order to help them to make better use of the National Housing Act. (Text):

I should like to make a few suggestions during the passing of the estimates of the Minister of Public Works. Recently in a Vancouver paper there appeared an article written by Mr. Cliff MacKay, the financial critic, and it said this:
Signs indicate that this country needs a five-year plan of economic redevelopment. Cities can and do have five-year plans to clear slums or channel traffic. But the nation itself seems to he chained to an economic system based on a 365-day budget with an occasional baby budget thrown in to tinker with the more obvious mistakes.
It went on to ask what kind of way is that to deal with problems which have been building up ever since the end of the last war. The main suggestion that the editor is making here is that there should be a comprehensive five-year plan for proper economic development. Prior to the appearance of that article in the Vancouver paper, I had a similar plan in mind and I took time to write a 24-page report which I called a seven-year program for appropriate development of a number of projects in the Vancouver area. I am not going to deal exhaustively with that lengthy report at this time. However I wish to say that I would appreciate having, at an early date, an interview with the minister's officials in order to discuss this very lengthy document. I feel that many of the suggestions contained in the report would be most welcome in my area. The report deals with a number of projects in which the federal government already has an interest in the city of Vancouver. The report deals with a proper long range development of the Jericho beach area and also with the proper development of an area in which the R.C.A.F. at present carries on operations at the south end of Burrard bridge. My report deals with the re-activation of the Boundary Bay airport, an area which is much needed by small plane owners in the city of Vancouver and

surrounding areas. The report also deals with the much needed all-purpose coliseum which would be of major interest to the Department of Trade and Commerce. The report also deals with the necessity of housing the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation under one roof in the city of Vancouver. At the present time the operations of the corporation are carried on in some six different buildings in a most uneconomic fashion. The report which I drafted also deals with the unification of the network of railroad lines which lead into the Vancouver area and it sets forth what the Canadian National Railway Company and the Great Northern Railway Company could do, for example, in uniting their present depot. The report also deals with the international airport, a matter which I hope the ratepayers of the city of Vancouver will resolve this coming week.
In particular I should like to deal with another breakwater in addition to the one which was referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver East today. He spoke about a much needed breakwater and I support his remarks to the fullest extent. We need, the San Juan breakwater on Vancouver island. However, at the same time we also need a breakwater which has been long advocated by many people in the Vancouver area. I refer to a breakwater which is to be constructed either at Locarno beach or to the east of Jericho beach or closer in to the downtown area at the south end of the Burrard bridge.
We are a port city. Our people go down to the sea in ships. Every winter and certainly every spring pictures appear on the front pages of our newspapers showing small craft that have been washed ashore during a sudden squall. Every time those pictures appear, the city officials again suggest and1 cry out for a proper breakwater. There is an ever increasing number of small craft owners. In a city which will have approximately one and half million people by 1980, according to what the forecasters say, we certainly need now and will need even more in the future a proper breakwater in the area to which I have referred. In correspondence with the minister's department it was reported as follows:
Tentative studies have been carried out on such a project and two sites were actively considered. They were at Jericho beach and Spanish banks. The Spanish banks site had been more particularly referred to as the Locarno beach area. The tentative plans call for a combination rock and sand fill of about 2,000 feet in length starting from the shore near Blanca street, then carrying a rock mound parallel to the shore and eastward to a point in front of Locarno Park. The area behind this protection would be dredged for floats and a mooring basin. The plans call for accommodation for approximately 1,500 boats.
Supply-Public Works
The previous minister of public works, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs, indicated that the senior government would contribute $1 million to the construction of the breakwater to which I have referred. I do hope that when the minister is commenting upon this proposed breakwater he will once again say, as his predecessor said, that the $1 million is still available provided, of course, that the city of Vancouver and the province of British Columbia make an equal contribution. At least if we have his assurance that the $1 million is available from the federal government we will continue to press for equal grants from the province of British Columbia and from the city of Vancouver.
I do not necessarily advocate that the breakwater be located at Jericho beach or Spanish banks, or even near the south end of Burrard bridge, but I do strongly recommend that we have a breakwater on the south side of English bay. The Kitsilano ratepayers' association, which is an association in my own riding, passed a resolution as follows:
That the Kitsilano ratepayers' association go on record as supporting the proposed breakwater at Locarno beach with a marina for small boats.
There has been an impressive number of other organizations recommending the construction of a breakwater in this area. Therefore I hope the minister will say that the senior government is still prepared to make a contribution of $1 million toward that much needed project.
Then there is another matter which comes within the minister's field concerning the False creek area, which is in the Burrard riding. The problem of the proper development of the False creek area has been under consideration for some 30 years and I would like to feel that during the time I am able to represent the Vancouver-Burrard riding suitable progress will be made in the appropriate development of False creek.
This area has been praised as a secondary harbour with first-class industrial sites, and it has been damned as a polluted waterway and an ugly and dirty eyesore that should be, according to some, eliminated once and for all by filling it in. Its shores are lined by industry, as the minister knows, and harbour experts say it is on the whole poorly laid out; land is being used to a fraction of its potential, which means not only a loss of good sites and misuse of a potentially good waterway, but a loss of tax revenue to the city.
The minister's department comes into this project because there is a considerable amount of dredging to be done in order that we can properly develop this secondary harbour in Vancouver. It is necessary, so the planners

Supply-Public Works
say, to establish a 300-foot channel and development of industrial sites up to that channel as part of a long range program. As I see it, the factors which make False creek a target for criticism at the present time are:
1.	There is inefficient and uneconomical use of the land which is considered prime industrial property with road, rail and water service.
2.	The road system around it and into it is inadequate.
3.	The old Kitsilano trestle located just east of Burrard bridge blocks the False creek entrance to all but small boats. There is only IJt feet of water at the swing span at low tide and deep dredging is impossible. This railway bridge was the first creek crossing, was finished in 1886 and is still used by the B.C. electric railway.
4.	The water is polluted and this area, bordering on the downtown and spanned by major traffic routes, is an eyesore.
I understand that the minister's department has carried on extensive dredging operations in that area during the past year. I hope that when this item comes up for consideration later in the minister's estimates he will indicate what the dredging operation has proved so that we can now properly plan the future development of the False creek area.
I would also like to feel that the minister and the other appropriate minister concerned will in due time consent to a change of name for False creek. The name which I suggest is Kitsilano bay or Kitsilano harbour. I sometimes have difficulty, because its name is False creek, in conveying to the officials of the Department of Public Works that it is in fact playing a very useful purpose in the Vancouver area and will in the future play an even more important role as Vancouver's secondary harbour.
If because of the fact that there is a hodgepodge of interests in the whole area agreement cannot be reached among the ownerships, I suggest that perhaps the only answer may be for the government to take action and assume power similar to that in relation to metropolitan areas and proceed to set up a commission to get the job done. Possibly some public authority should be set up at an early date in order that there can be proper development of the area. Mr. Chairman, may I call it five o'clock?

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-18, to incorporate Ukrainian Evangelical Baptist Convention of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to me to have the honour of sponsoring this bill in this house. I should like to inform hon. members briefly of the work of the Ukrainian Evangelical Baptist Convention.
The work of Ukrainian Baptists in Canada began in Winnipeg in 1902. As immigrants from the Ukraine flowed into Canada from the year 1900 onward, further churches were established, in western Canada at first, and later on in other parts of the country. The convention of Canada has two local conferences, one with its centre in eastern Canada and the other with its centre in western Canada. The headquarters of the conference in the east are at Toronto and the headquarters of the conference in the west are at Saskatoon. The convention represents more than 7,000 Baptists of Ukrainian origin. There are more than 500 pupils attending Sunday schools conducted by the convention. There are 21 organized churches, with an adult membership of more than 800. In addition there are some 25 mission stations where services are held periodically. There are 10 ordained ministers and 10 missionaries.
The churches are located as follows: One in Montreal, Quebec; five in Ontario; three in Manitoba; three in Saskatchewan; six in Alberta, and three in British Columbia. The mission stations are scattered throughout Canada.
The convention owns a periodical called the Christian Herald, which is the organ of the convention. It is published in Winnipeg.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills.

the second reading of Bill No. S-25, respecting the Canada Permanent Trust Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to authorize the Canada Permanent Trust Company to merge and amalgamate with the Toronto General Trusts Corporation and to authorize Canada Permanent Mortgage Corporation, which holds all of the shares of the Canada Permanent Trust Company except directors' qualifying shares, to invest in the whole or any portion of the shares 
of the amalgamated company and to exchange shares of the Canada Permanent Trust Company for shares of the amalgamated company.
General legislation enabling such an amalgamation to take place is provided for in the loan and trust corporation act, chapter 222 of the revised statutes of Ontario, 1960, but no corresponding general legislation has as yet been enacted by parliament. The enactment of the present bill is therefore necessary before the proposed amalgamation may be effected.
It may be of interest to note that the parent body of the Canada Permanent Trust Company, namely the Canada Permanent Mortgage Corporation, was incorporated in 1885 under the British building societies act of upper Canada with the name of Canada Permanent Building and Savings Society. Later, by a special act of the parliament of Canada passed in 1899, the parent company was incorporated with the name Canada Permanent and Western Canada Corporation. Then in 1927 this company acquired the assets of the Brantford Trust Company and in 1949 acquired the assets and business of the General Trust and Executors Corporation of Halifax. At the present time it is known as the Canada Permanent Trust Corporation, which has an authorized capital of $15 million, of which $2 million has been fully paid up.
The Toronto General Trust Company was first incorporated in 1872 by act of the provincial legislature of Ontario. However, this Company did not commence business operations until February 3, 1882. These two companies have had a lengthy period in the financial operations of this country. I understand that the locations of these corporations complement each other in that by the amalgamation there will not be very much duplication of offices and in that in the area where there are no Canada Permanent Trust offices there are Toronto General Trust offices.
I suggest that if there are any questions to be asked they could better be asked in committee.
Will the hon. member permit a question. What will be the name of the new firm?
This is shown in clause 1 of the present bill. It is the Canada Permanent Toronto General Trust Company. The French name will be Compagnie de Fiducie Canada Permanent Toronto General.

Mr. Speaker, again the use of the word "Canada" may give people the impression that this is a company under the control of the government. There is a danger in that and I would oppose the use of the

word "Canada" in the name of the new company. If it was an old company and was still in existence and was to carry on I would not object; but I think the word "Canada" or the words "National Canadian" or anything of that kind should not be in the name of any corporation so that people would not get the impression that the corporation belonged to the government of Canada. For this reason I believe we should ask the company to change the name so that it will be acceptable to everyone.
I suggest that this can be discussed fully in committee.

It was my
understanding that the hon. member for Davenport would not be in the position of closing the debate. I saw, sir, that you had not stirred yourself and therefore I thought I was fully protected.
I notice in the bill, Mr. Speaker, there are some of what one might consider to be protective devices, in that the legislation does not come into effect except upon proclamation by the governor in council, following tests to be made by the government of the province of Ontario and assented to by the lieutenant governor of that province. Therefore I feel it will be some little time yet before the actual amalgamating company which is named in the bill can come into being.
I think this is something that should be dealt with at this time, Mr. Speaker, in a preliminary way before it goes to the committee. I took the trouble to look into the Financial Post survey of industrials for 1960 to see what the relative positions of the two companies, the Canada Permanent Trust Company and the Toronto General Trusts Corporation, were with respect to the trust companies structure in Canada. We And that in the year 1959 the total assets listed for the Canada Permanent Trust were $177,493,368. The total assets of the other trust corporation which is mentioned in the bill, which will be a party to the agreement, were in 1959, $576,547,704. Once these companies have amalgamated and without taking into account the relationship which the third parent company, that is Canada Permanent Mortgage Corporation, will have, but taking into account only these two firms or companies which are to amalgamate, we see their total assets in 1959-undoubtedly they are larger now- are $754,041,012, or about three quarters of a billion dollars in total assets.
In the last couple of years we have seen two or three other mergers, amalgamations or acquisitions of one company by another in the trust company field. For instance, in 1958 Western Trust Company was acquired by

Guaranty Trust. In 1959 Okanagan Trust Company was acquired by Royal Trust. I think this will perhaps be the third amalgamation or merger in the trust company field in the last two or three years. It would place the amalgamated company sought to be established by the bill in the position of being at least the third or, depending on its relationship with the Canada Permanent Mortgage Company, perhaps the second largest trust company in Canada in terms of listed assets.
I should like to give some indication of what would be the relative positions of these two or three larger companies of which the amalgamated company would be one. In the 1960 Financial Post survey of industrials some 28 companies are listed in the trust company field, and following this merger there would be 27. Of the total of 27 and taking into account what is proposed under the bill, we find that three of them, the amalgamated company, the Royal Trust Company and the National Trust Company will have assets greater than those of all the other trust companies combined. Thus, in terms of their assets, these three companies will be in a rather powerful position compared with all the other companies.
I worked out the figures very roughly and I have them here. The total of 28 companies last year had assets of approximately $6,200 million and the amalgamated company to be established under the bill, the Royal Trust Company and the National Trust Company will have assets of approximately $3,800 million.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.

I think the hon. member will agree with me, and I suggest he might make this point, that when he speaks of the assets of these companies the vast bulk of these assets belong to other people and are merely held by these companies as trustee or agent, involving no ownership on their part.

I quite agree that that is probably correct. One of the purposes of a trust company is to hold things in trust for other people. I was not saying that these were earned assets as in the case of life insurance companies. I was pointing out that in terms of assets held these three companies will be in the position of having total assets greater than the total assets of the 24 other companies in Canada taken together, as shown in the 1960 Financial Post survey of industrials.

Private Bills
The survey also lists loan companies alongside trust companies and there is a relationship between loan companies and trust companies. With respect to the bill before us, there is a relationship in that, as is mentioned in the bill, the Canada Permanent Mortgage Corporation holds all of the shares of the Canada Permanent Trust Company except directors' qualifying shares. In looking at the list in the Financial Post survey I see there are cross-references as to holdings by one company in another. The Royal Trust Company is not isolated from the loan company in that one lends money and the other holds money in trust because I understand that a trust company holding money in trust is able to invest in certain types of securities in some instances which brings a return to the person for whom they hold the money in trust.
The point is that in the past few years there has been one merger after another of trust companies and we now have another which will result in the National Trust Company, the Royal Trust Company and the amalgamated company having assets greater than the assets of all the other companies taken together. I am wondering whether this is not a matter that should be explored rather fully in the committee. We certainly explore these things through the combines investigation branch under the Combines Investigation Act although the act does not cover the field of finance with the exception of insurance rates. The provision of services, as it were, and loans are excluded from the Combines Investigation Act although the act deals with monopolies, oligopolies and price fixing situations in the field of commodities and sales.
I wonder whether this is not something that the committee should not explore more fully to see whether we are getting into a dangerous position in Canada. I think that this perhaps should be done when we find three corporations of this type with assets more than all the others put together and when we are moving more and more towards larger and larger trust companies with the number of active trust companies becoming less and less.
I do not raise this matter in the same way as I would if the corporation involved were in the field of production and sale of commodities or consumer goods or something of that nature. I think this matter is in a different field but it concerns the money of individuals. In one case they entrust their money and in the other case they buy something. In the one case prices may be fixed by arrangement and in the other case some mutually agreeable arrangement may be worked out which is not truly beneficial to

the financial situation in Canada. I am not trying to say that in this instance I see arriving on the scene some huge corporate octopus which is going to engulf the entire financial field or drive other trust companies out of business by acquisitions, mergers and the like, eventually leading to a situation where only a few companies have practically all the trust assets in Canada.
I raise this matter because I think it should be considered by the committee. There is a move here in the same direction that has taken place in other fields involving mergers such as the sugar industry, the beer industry and so on. There is a move in the direction of larger companies, greater assets and a smaller and smaller number of companies with the concentration of authority, as it were, in the hands of fewer and fewer people. I think this matter must be looked at rather seriously from the point of view of ensuring that the interests of people who have money with trust companies and the interests of the country as a whole are protected to the fullest extent possible.
The growth of monopolies and oligopolies is not always detrimental. A monopoly per se is not detrimental but the manner in which it operates may be. These are some things that I think should be looked at seriously by the committee to ensure that the trust company situation in the financial world is protected, that these other relationships are protected to the fullest extent possible, that investors are protected and that the general public are also protected. These various interests should be protected from activities that might be directed-I am not saying they will be-toward controlling more and more such assets, activities which are not in keeping with the good sense that we now expect of trust companies.
When the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton) introduced the bill, he said that it would allow the amalgamated company to have offices that will fairly well cover the country. I understand that one company now has offices in one area and another company in another area. The bill will allow the amalgamated company to carry on operations in a broad field. I would certainly appreciate from the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton), who is sponsoring the bill and who has a knowledge of the corporate structure of trust companies, some indication of his views on what I have said, namely whether or not when the officials of the company are before the committee they will be prepared to deal with this specific point.

should like to make one comment on the remarks made by the hon. member for Hull

(Mr. Caron) with regard to the use of "Canada" in the name. I do sympathize with him in the feeling he has that the name should be safeguarded and that it can, on occasion, give rise to misunderstandings. I would submit, however, for his consideration that in this case it is somewhat different. The Canada Permanent has had the name "Canada" for nearly a century now and it would, therefore, be very confusing and indeed a rather serious matter to ask a company with such a long time and honourably known name to change it. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is rather ironical that I should have the opportunity this afternoon to say a few words about a company such as the Canada Permanent Trust Company. My early recollection of this company is rather unfavourable. Certainly if I had been asked 25 years ago to support this measure, I would have turned it down without any questions asked.
I should like, however, to refer to the situation which produced this feeling. My first association with this company was when we bought a farm from that organization. This was during the depths of the depression, and the farm had originally had a mortgage against it for a small amount. However, because of the structure of this company, they compounded the interest on the amounts that were due and before long there was $10,000 owing on this farm. If this is still the practice of this company, the committee should give some consideration to it because I am still opposed to it. Fortunately, my father was able to obtain a loan and we bought the farm at a lower price than that amount.
As I say, this incident occurred in the depths of the depression. Probably the relationships of the farmers and the Canada Permanent Trust Company in northern Ontario were highly unsatisfactory. People who had homesteaded farms and who had borrowed small amounts of money on these farms, then found that the interest was compounded at a time when payments were not made, and were not being made anywhere across the country. Those people who had mortgages with Canada Permanent Trust Company, because of this practice of compounding the interest, in most cases lost their farms. At one time this company probably had as much farm land in my area as was owned by all the farmers put together.

This company seems to be expanding rather quickly. Their net earnings have been something over 11| per cent. This would seem to indicate a very healthy situation at a time when repossessions are probably small in number and when defaults on payments are very small. I believe the committee would be well advised to look into this matter of compounding the interest on arrears. If this is still the policy of this company, then I believe the committee should take steps to see that the matter is corrected. We have now a much more humane method of handling this situation in so far as other kinds of financing are concerned. It would seem to me that we could develop, without much difficulty, a much better system than this compounding of interest. It was not advantageous to the farmers in my area, and I am sure it was not advantageous to the Canada Permanent because, while the farmer lost his farm the Canada Permanent lost its reputation and a great deal of money in that area. The company has not returned to the area to any extent since the depression.
For these reasons, I believe the committee should give consideration to this matter. I am unable to say whether or not the Guaranty Trust has followed this practice. However, I feel that when these companies are asking parliament to increase the amount of mortgage money under their control, then we should be very cautious about permitting a practice that has, in the past, had serious repercussions. In my opinion, this practice has created hardship for the mortgagee through no fault of his own. He was not responsible for causing the depression. In my area, many people who had homesteaded, built their own farms, lost them, even though the amount owing was small, because of this practice of compounding the interest on the arrears.
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I do not see anything in this bill concerning interest rates, and I wonder if the hon. member is not straying a little from the subject.

the second reading of Bill No. S-27, respecting Guaranty Trust Company of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to authorize an increase in the capital stock of the company from $5 million to $10 million. I believe also in clause 2 permission is given to the company to use, in addition to the name of Guaranty Trust Company of Canada, the name Compagnie Guaranty Trust du Canada, which is the French version of their name. This company is a wholly owned Canadian company. It has over 2,200 shareholder residents in Canada from coast to coast. It was first founded and started business in 1925 after incorporation in Windsor, Ontario. The company continued to operate with one office until 1934, when it chose the most important city in Canada, namely the city of Toronto,-perhaps I should not put it that way-in which to open its second office. The company operated two offices until 1940 when it acquired the assets of the Fidelity Trust Company of Ontario which had an office in Niagara Falls. This acquisition provided the company with a third office in the province of Ontario. Since that time the company has grown. The company now has 15 active offices. It hopes to extend its operations before the end of the current year and that it will have 20 offices. At the present time there are approximately 300 employees on the payroll and additional employees, of course, will be added. This company has also participated in taking mortgages under the National Housing Act. I understand they hold in excess of $27 million in mortgages which have been acquired under this act over a period of time. If there are any questions that any of the members would like to ask

concerning this company now, or in the committee, I shall be glad to try to answer them.
Before the hon. member takes his seat I wonder whether he can answer two questions. One is this. What page is he reading from?
I was referring to some of the notes that were taken from the proceedings of the other place, at page 769.
Can the hon. member also indicate what is the par value of the shares?

It would appear that originally the shares of this company had a par value of $100; but in 1949 these shares were split, 10 for one, into shares having a par value of $10. This was done in order to permit a wider distribution of ownership in the company by small investors in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, before you put the question may I say this. As may be recalled, just by way of accident more than anything else, this is one of the companies I mentioned when we were considering Bill S-25. I mentioned it then, in an incidental way; and as I say, just by coincidence, the same company happens to have reference here. May I say first that earlier the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton) as I understand him, in effect said yes, that we should concern ourselves about the growth of monopolies and the like but that it was not of too much concern at the moment; that perhaps after a while, if it got to be a problem of fewer and fewer companies in this field controlling more and more assets, then we should concern ourselves about it. He said it really was not a problem at this time. That is generally what I understood him to say.
While it may not be a problem at this time -and I am not suggesting that it is a problem, apart from the fact that, as I said, three companies own more assets than do all the other 24 put together which fact to me puts them in a unique and powerful position-I think it is something that we should continue to keep under review, especially in this field where the combines investigation branch has relatively little jurisdiction apart, as I understand it, from the question of insurance itself as a service. The rest of its activities are in the commodities and con-summer goods fields and relate to price fixing and other unfair trade practices.
This particular company acquired Western Trust Company in 1958, so it is a company which is into this field of merging and it is one with which we should concern ourselves. Its growth as a company is demonstrated by the fact that originally the shares
Private Bills
were at $100 par value and were then split ten to one. One of the reasons given by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton) was that this allowed small investors to invest in the company. This is somewhat the same reason that is given for other companies splitting shares, except that they relate theirs to their market value. Then when the shares get too high on the market it does not look good for them to have it that way and they engage in a stock splitting business to make it look as though the company is not faring very well and is just holding its own.
I would imagine the Guaranty Trust Company has done relatively well over the years. In fact, according to the 1960 survey of industrials, in 1959 it had total assets of some $220 million. It does not indicate in here, except perhaps by way of subtraction, what the assets were of Western Trust Company which was acquired a year before, but we notice that in the one year period the assets of this company increased by some $35 million. Whether or not this reflects the position of Western Trust Company is very, very difficult to say. However, in 1957 it had assets of $142 million. Therefore in one year we see a jump of about $40 million in assets, and the next year an approximate increase of $35 million in total assets, with earnings per share running around $2-$1.95 to be exact.
We should look at this question in terms of the growth of the corporate structure, and I think we must all be on guard to ensure that in fact these groups do not become laws unto themselves outside of the operation and the control of parliament, which is really the only agency which is able in any marked degree to protect individual members of society against the hugeness of the corporate structure.
The purpose of this bill being to double the capital stock of the company-which is in fact what it does by increasing it from $5 million to $10 million-indicates to me that perhaps Guaranty Trust has a good perception of what may exist in the future, because I am sure they do not want just to double their capital stock for the fun of it; there must be some purpose behind doing this sort of thing.
It would be interesting to find out just what this particular company has in mind in doubling its share capital because, as I have said, it seems to have been doing fairly well under the old capitalization of $5 million, which I gather has been in existence since 1925, although I may have misread the explanatory notes. Since 1925 the company has had a $5 million capital structure. During that period of time it has built up these assets in a rather marked degree. As shown

Business of the House
by the survey ol industrials, over the last two year period this company has increased its total assets from $142 million to $220 million, or almost an $80 million increase. This represents a 50 per cent or 60 per cent increase in total assets over a two year period.
I think that if we looked at the figures of this company next year we might find it is in an even more advantageous position and anticipates quite an additional growth in its assets. This would mean that the more this company grows, the more it will be brought into relationship with the three companies I mentioned earlier, and perhaps the four of them will control even larger and larger amounts of the total assets of all the trust companies in existence in Canada.
I think this is something we should continue to be on guard against to ensure that the corporate structure does not get into the position of being a private law unto itself, with the individual having relatively little protection against its activities.
